We propose the DAS4AIC to operationalise the 20 AI assurance precepts throughout capability development and sustainment. Further, we demonstrate how classical safety precepts map from human-dominant assurance through software-dominant assurance to the assurance of AI-enabled systems with conceptual validation. Our preliminary evaluation is that some human assurance precepts map more directly to AI-enabled systems than through the intermediate step of software assurance, suggesting that established human assurance concepts may have continuing relevance for AI-enabled capabilities. To our knowledge, this is the first study to align emerging AI-assurance precepts explicitly with the earlier and still overlapping, human-dominant and software-dominant assurance paradigms.

title: Momentum-Based Byzantine-Resilient Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization with Different Batch Sizes Across Different Clients
abstract: In recent years, many studies have focused on the robustness of federated learning (FL) systems against Byzantine attacks. Prior work has shown that integrating stochastic optimization algorithms with momentum can effectively enhance the robustness, particularly in non-convex scenarios. However, most studies assume a fixed batch size across all workers, which may not be suitable for practical deployments. In this study, we investigate the impact of different batch sizes across different clients on Byzantine robustness in FL. Specifically, we propose a weighted aggregation framework (WAggF), which assigns different weights to gradients received from different clients. WAggF can be easily embedded into various aggregation rules to boost Byzantine resilience. We further establish theoretical convergence guarantees for two momentum-based stochastic optimization algorithms&mdash;Byz-WNSGDM and Byz-EF21-WSGDM&mdash;under WAggF. To reduce communication overhead and enable synchronous training, we incorporate a contractive compressor (which encompasses Top-K as a special case) into the stochastic optimization algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed algorithms consistently improve robustness against a range of Byzantine attacks.

title: Summer Maize Leaf Area Index Estimation Using Approximate Days After Sowing and Dual-Domain Paired-Difference Features
abstract: Residue-soil mixing and reduced spectral sensitivity complicate summer maize leaf area index (LAI) estimation from unmanned aerial vehicle multispectral imagery. We compared full-plot and canopy domains, paired differences, neighborhood statistics, and approximate days after sowing (DAS), calculated from a common reference date. Five input schemes (B0&ndash;B4) and four algorithms were evaluated using 345 samples collected on five dates in one growing season. Spatial validation comprised ten repetitions of five-fold grouped cross-validation, with preprocessing and feature selection restricted to training data. For gradient boosting decision trees, R2 increased from 0.515 for B0 to 0.686 for B3 and 0.846 for B4, whereas RMSE decreased from 0.834 to 0.671 and 0.470. Low-LAI Bias decreased from 0.580 to 0.343 and 0.160. Fixed-capacity controls supported conditional improvements after adding paired differences and neighborhood statistics. Approximate DAS produced the largest sequential RMSE reduction, mainly through between-date adjustment. Time-baseline and training-fold residual analyses distinguish calendar-time adjustment from within-date predictive information. High-LAI underestimation and unseen-date errors delimit application beyond the sampled dates and production-field conditions. Within this defined scope, the framework provides a reproducible comparison of image-domain representations under heterogeneous production conditions.

title: Explainability for Forecasting Task with Close-Up Option
abstract: Although machine learning-based forecasting models often function as opaque black boxes, explainability methods provide the essential tools required to foster trust in deep learning systems, optimize computational resources, and enhance model accuracy. Motivated by this, we propose a model-agnostic, local explainability method specifically designed for forecasting tasks. Our approach employs a hierarchical structure that is generated iteratively. From the outset, a small number of &ldquo;interpretable components&rdquo; that decompose the input are considered. In the inductive step, the methodology enables analysts to examine the data in greater detail, allowing for a deeper exploration of specific subcomponents whenever a higher resolution is required. This framework inherently provides control over computational costs by tuning the branching factor. The resulting explainability tree shares certain, but not all, properties of the explainability values provided by the SHAP-LIME framework; in this regard, we present some theoretical results. Furthermore, numerical experiments provided evidence that explanation coherence is fundamentally maintained between both methods. We explored the utility of this methodology on a real-world short-term load forecasting LSTM encoder&ndash;decoder model.

title: WarfaRisk: A Reproducible, Fairness-Aware Machine Learning Pipeline for Warfarin Dose Prediction (Prototype)
abstract: Warfarin dosing is complicated by wide inter-patient variability driven by genetic, demographic, and pharmacological factors. Although machine learning approaches to dose prediction have been widely studied, published evaluations are frequently affected by analysis-domain data leakage, small held-out sets, and an absence of calibration and fairness assessment across ancestry subgroups. We describe WarfaRisk, a nine-phase open-source machine learning pipeline for warfarin dose prediction evaluated on two public International Warfarin Pharmacogenetics Consortium (IWPC) cohorts (n=6037 and n=1780, the latter a non-independent secondary consistency check) using fixed patient-level splits and a single documented random seed. The pipeline incorporates leakage-free preprocessing, nested clinical and pharmacogenomic feature ablation across nine model architectures, leave-one-ancestry-out portability assessment with a cross-model robustness check, conformal prediction calibration reported at subgroup resolution, and individual-level SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) feature attribution. The nine-architecture ablation results reported here are from the primary cohort, IWPC-6256; the complete two-cohort comparison is reported in a companion evaluation manuscript. A prototype web-based clinical decision support interface integrates dose recommendation, uncertainty quantification, and SHAP explainability with a Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) R4 endpoint. In preliminary evaluation on a single fixed held-out split, Model Agnostic Prediction Interval Estimator (MAPIE) cross-conformal (5-fold CV+) prediction achieves coverage close to its nominal target when measured across each cohort as a whole. When this coverage is instead stratified by ancestry, a different pattern emerges: coverage for African-ancestry patients falls well short, a gap the aggregate number hides, plausibly explained by alleles missing from the standard IWPC genotype panel and supported by independent pharmacogenetic literature, though not directly demonstrated in this dataset. These findings indicate that subgroup-level calibration reporting is necessary, not optional, since its absence can let a model appear well-calibrated in aggregate while failing a specific population in practice.

title: Two-Stage Attention-Based Insertion Policy for the Dynamic Vehicle Routing Problem
abstract: This paper addresses dynamic vehicle routing with online requests, where insertion heuristics follow fixed rules ignoring the effect of each insertion on later requests. It proposes a two-stage attention-based insertion policy: a first stage selects a vehicle, and a second stage an insertion position within its route. Routes and fleet are encoded by attention, and the policy is trained with REINFORCE and a greedy rollout baseline on the final episode cost instead of immediate insertion costs. It is compared with cheapest, nearest and random insertion and with a single-stage policy over all vehicle&ndash;position pairs, on instances with 10 to 120 customers and degrees of dynamism from 10% to 90%. Both learned policies outperform nearest and random insertion and generalize to unseen sizes and degrees of dynamism. When most customers are dynamic on instances with up to 35 customers, the single-stage policy outperforms cheapest insertion by up to 3.1% and the two-stage policy matches it; otherwise, cheapest insertion remains better. The single-stage policy is cheaper in most settings, but the two-stage policy decides up to 2.7 and trains up to 5.7 times faster, for a cost at most 3.6% higher, and becomes cheaper on large, highly dynamic instances.

title: Exploring Romanian Misinformation with GraphRAG: Community-Level Narratives of COVID-19
abstract: Predefined thematic taxonomies can obscure how misinformation narratives emerge, overlap, and change over time. One way to address this limitation is by developing bottom-up data-driven approaches that identify narratives directly from data. We present a pipeline that extracts entities and relations from news articles using GraphRAG, identifies communities using the Leiden algorithm, and uses this information to explore and predict misinformation. We evaluate the pipeline on a set of Romanian COVID-19 pandemic news articles with expert-defined narrative annotations and adapt the extraction prompts to Romanian. Exploratory results show that in this corpus, the graph for fake news is more fragmented and less modular than the graph for real news; it also contains higher proportions of events, disinformation theory, and vaccine entities, whereas the real-news graph contains higher proportions of locations, hospitals, and public health measures. Communities in the combined graph align weakly with the predefined super-narrative labels, indicating that the two representations group articles differently. Furthermore, expert review of similar articles from communities identified within the combined real&ndash;fake graph suggests that an approach based on entity and community may offer a promising avenue for identifying subtle misinformation strategies. Regarding the prediction task, a three-component ensemble that uses graph information achieves 85.86% macro-F1 (95% CI [78.50, 91.27]) and 86.51% accuracy (95% CI [78.57, 91.27]) on classifying articles as fake or true. These point estimates suggest incremental gains over the two-component ensemble without the graph similarity signal, though these gains are not statistically confirmed at this sample size. Together, these exploratory results illustrate the use of GraphRAG as a tool in pipelines that support the exploration and prediction of misinformation.

title: From Anthropomorphism to Trust: Unpacking the Role of Authenticity in Generative AI and Large Language Models&mdash;A Structured Literature Review and Future Research Agenda
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has changed the conditions under which users encounter and evaluate machine-produced communication. In systems based on large language models, conversational output is no longer merely functional; it can be fluent, context-aware, and socially legible, inviting judgments that extend beyond usefulness, accuracy, or efficiency. Yet the literature still tends to treat anthropomorphism, perceived authenticity, and trust as largely separate constructs, without sufficiently explaining how human-like cues become credible in the eyes of users and how this credibility shapes trust. To address this problem, the present structured literature review synthesizes recent research on anthropomorphism, authenticity-related evaluations, and trust in AI-mediated interaction, with particular attention to conversational AI, generative AI, and LLM-based systems. A structured search in the Web of Science Core Collection identified 655 records; after duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 96 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The analysis identifies several interrelated thematic patterns, including anthropomorphic cues and social presence, authenticity-related mechanisms in AI-mediated communication, trust formation and calibration, boundary conditions, and behavioral responses to conversational AI. On this basis, the review develops an integrative conceptual framework and proposes perceived anthropomorphic authenticity as a review-derived construct for examining how users evaluate human-like AI communication in relation to trust. The study contributes to human&ndash;AI interaction research by clarifying the role of authenticity-related evaluations between anthropomorphic cues and calibrated trust and by identifying conditions under which human-like communication may be associated with trust, skepticism, overreliance, or trust erosion.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Blood Loss from Arterial Waveform Feature Analysis in a Nonhuman Primate Hemorrhage Model
abstract: Hemorrhage is the leading cause of preventable death in trauma, yet traditional vital signs can fail to detect early blood loss due to physiological compensatory mechanisms. Objective, continuous monitoring of hemorrhage progression remains an unmet clinical need. This study developed and validated a machine learning model of percent estimated blood loss in a nonhuman primate hemorrhage model. Adult male baboons underwent controlled stepwise hemorrhage to approximately 25% blood loss while high-fidelity arterial waveform and blood loss data were captured. Morphological waveform features were extracted, and a Gradient Boosting model was developed using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. A 10 s window with 10 features achieved a mean coefficient of determination of 0.81 and mean absolute error of 2.5%. On three independently held-out subjects, per-subject coefficient of determination ranged from 0.75 to 0.94 while mean absolute error ranged from 1.4% to 3.3%. Notably, percent estimated blood loss detected hemorrhage a median of 8.1 min before sustained blood pressure decline, at approximately 7% blood loss while systolic pressure remained stable. These findings indicate that arterial waveform morphology can enable accurate, continuous blood loss estimation and may provide early warning before hemorrhage becomes detectable through conventional vital sign monitoring in this preclinical model.

title: FA-DGNet: Pseudo-Supervised Difficulty-Aware Learning and Guided Refinement for Colonoscopic Polyp Segmentation
abstract: Colonoscopy is a crucial method for colorectal cancer screening and the early detection of precancerous polyps; however, accurate polyp segmentation is challenged by factors such as indistinct boundaries, minute or flat structures, and regions of high-intensity interference. Given the spatial variability of these challenges, we propose FA-DGNet, a polyp-segmentation model built upon the HarDNet-68 backbone that integrates &ldquo;pseudo-supervised difficulty learning&rdquo; with &ldquo;guided refinement&rdquo; strategies. The model employs a deterministic training objective that incorporates dilated mask boundaries, locally sparse foreground regions, and brightness-inferred areas prone to artifacts, all without requiring additional manual annotations. The learned difficulty response modulates two stages of the decoder via a bounded residual amplification mechanism, while auxiliary supervision is provided by dedicated artifact and edge detection heads. On the Kvasir-SEG dataset, FA-DGNet achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.9071 and a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.8508, outperforming the baseline model&rsquo;s metrics of 0.9006 and 0.8418, respectively. Furthermore, cross-dataset transfer experiments and evaluations across five independent test sets confirmed the model&rsquo;s generalization capability and performance stability. Static performance analysis indicates that the model incurs only marginal increases of approximately 0.43% in active parameters and 0.45% in multiply&ndash;accumulate (MAC) operations. Overall, FA-DGNet offers a low-overhead, difficulty-aware optimization strategy, providing a practical solution for colonoscopic polyp segmentation.

title: Cryptanalysis and Improvement of an Image Cryptosystem via Chaotic Synchronization and Artificial Neural Networks in Modified OTP Scheme
abstract: Chaos-based image ciphers may exhibit favorable statistical metrics while retaining a recoverable algebraic structure. We analyze the modified one-time-pad image cryptosystem of Stoycheva et al., which combines static, Chua-system-derived, and neural masks with channel-wise shuffling and XOR. For observations sharing a fixed or reproduced induced state, we prove that each color channel is equivalent to a plaintext-independent permutation followed by an XOR keystream. The trained neural component supplies a mask but does not alter this external structure. Established base-256 position labels recover the complete equivalent mapping with four chosen-plaintext queries for a 512-by-512 image; known-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext, differential, and black-box analyses are evaluated under explicitly stated access conditions. Under the same state, a one-byte plaintext difference changes exactly one ciphertext byte. We also specify a redesign that renews the three key components per image and couples cross-channel routing and masking to preceding ciphertext bytes. Its inverse is proved correct. Across 15 image&ndash;function trials, decryption was byte exact. Advancing the image counter changed 99.603907% of ciphertext bytes for the same image, and none of eight tested input pairs satisfied the fixed permutation&ndash;XOR affine identity. These results identify the state condition required by the recovery procedures and characterize the tested behavior of the redesigned image transformation.

title: When Does Representation Learning Help Attack-Path Forecasting? A Controlled Multi-Cloud Study with CAPTURE-MC
abstract: Cloud defenders increasingly want to anticipate an attacker&rsquo;s next move, not merely detect the last one. We study attack-path forecasting in multi-cloud environments: given the partial trace of an in-progress campaign, predict the next ATT&amp;CK technique. We present CAPTURE-MC, a heterogeneous temporal-graph model that encodes cross-provider telemetry and forecasts the next technique under a transition prior, and we release MC-PathBench, a synthetic but structurally faithful benchmark with four leakage-controlled generalization splits (temporal, cross-cloud, unseen-composition, and campaign hold-out). Our central contribution is an honest, carefully controlled account of when learned temporal-graph representations help and when they do not. We find that the technique-transition structure is a very strong predictor: when the attacker&rsquo;s current technique is known, a first-order Markov model and a uniform-over-allowed-transitions rule match or exceed CAPTURE-MC and a temporal-graph network, so the deep models add little in that idealized regime. The picture reverses in the realistic regime where the current technique must be inferred: as current-technique certainty degrades, the structural baselines, indexed entirely by it, collapse toward chance, whereas CAPTURE-MC degrades gracefully and nearly doubles their accuracy when the current technique is unknown. CAPTURE-MC is likewise robust to a substantially corrupted transition prior (missing, spurious, or misdirected edges). We also report, transparently, where CAPTURE-MC does not help: gradient-boosted trees remain the best per-event and campaign-level detectors; next-entity and time-to-transition prediction are at chance for every model; and the conformal layer, while achieving coverage, yields prediction sets larger than the list of allowed successors and so is not an efficiency gain. The prior is estimated only from training data, never the generator&rsquo;s graph, which removes a leakage path present in an earlier version of this work and changes several conclusions. The practical lesson for predictive cloud defense is that structural baselines are strong and must be reported, and that the value of representation learning appears precisely where structural assumptions break down.

title: Assessing Trustworthiness in LLMs-Assisted Literature Review: A Case Study of Multimodal Machine Learning in Medicine
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to support the structured extraction of methodological evidence from scientific literature and to build reviews and surveys. However, their use for scientific evidence extraction raises methodological questions concerning the consistency, correctness, and traceability of the extracted information. To address these aspects, this study assesses the trustworthiness of an LLM-assisted framework for structured methodological evidence extraction. A large-scale full-text corpus of multimodal machine learning in medicine, constructed through a structured literature search and automated open-access full-text retrieval, constitutes a case study for the evaluation. In this study, trustworthiness is operationalised through three complementary dimensions: extraction consistency, correctness, and traceability. The proposed pipeline was applied to 1371open-access full-text articles focused on multimodal machine learning in medicine. These articles were independently analysed using two locally deployed open-weight Large Language Models, Qwen and Gemma 3, through the same constrained prompt and predefined JSON schema. The extraction process was constrained through explicit anti-inference rules, while each structured item was linked to source-level textual evidence to support traceability and subsequent inspection. For selected research questions, extraction consistency was assessed through human inter-annotator agreement, whereas correctness was evaluated against an adjudicated human reference. Additional error analyses examined omissions, negative and Not specified outputs, while a targeted analysis conducted on a restricted subset of articles with Calibration-positive predictions examined the availability, textual fidelity, and methodological relevance of the associated source-linked evidence. Resultsare twofold: (i) methodologically, extraction reliability varied across tasks, with finer-grained categories showing lower positive recovery and more omissions; cross-model agreement alone was not sufficient to establish correctness; (ii) in the application case study, both models identified broadly consistent patterns across the analysed corpus, while datasets, fusion strategies, and reliability-oriented methods were frequently assigned to the Not specified category. Overall, the findings support the use of LLM-assisted extraction for large-scale methodological mapping, while highlighting the value of explicit assessment and human validation for interpreting model outputs.

title: A Variational Neural-Field Interpretation of the Stereo-CeNN Architecture in Light of Disparity-Tuned Cortical Organization
abstract: Stereoscopic vision relies on the ability of the visual system to estimate binocular disparity across the visual field. In computational models, stereo matching can be represented through multiple candidate disparity hypotheses defined over retinotopic position. In this work, we reinterpret the Stereo Cellular Neural Network, here referred to as Stereo-CeNN, within a continuous variational framework and introduce a neural-field representation defined over the joint domain of retinotopic position and disparity. In this interpretation, the discrete activities of the Stereo-CeNN are regarded as samples of a continuous activity field r(x,d,t), where different disparity layers correspond to populations tuned to different disparity preferences. The binocular input drives these populations according to local matching evidence, while spatial interactions within each disparity channel promote coherent activity across neighboring retinotopic locations. The final disparity estimate is obtained, consistently with the original Stereo-CeNN architecture, by selecting the disparity channel with the largest steady-state response at each retinotopic position. We show that the layer-wise organization and local spatial dynamics of the Stereo-CeNN admit a continuous neural-field counterpart, establishing an explicit structural and variational correspondence between the discrete retinotopy&ndash;disparity lattice and a population-level representation of stereopsis. This formulation provides a conceptual bridge between the independently developed Stereo-CeNN architecture and the mesoscale organization of disparity-selective populations observed in visual cortex, without implying a one-to-one anatomical or physiological correspondence. Because Cellular Neural Networks are locally connected dynamical systems originally conceived for analog and mixed-signal VLSI implementation, the same organization is also compatible with general neuromorphic principles of local, parallel, and distributed computation.

title: Impact of Class Imbalance Correction on Biological Feature Selection in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Methylation Data
abstract: Class imbalance is common in biomedical machine learning, yet imbalance-correction strategies are typically evaluated using predictive performance rather than their effects on biological interpretation. We evaluated six resampling methods: Random Oversampling (ROS), Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN), Random Undersampling (RUS), ClusterCentroids, and AllKNN (All K-Nearest Neighbors), together with a no-resampling baseline, using DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cohort. The analysis included 485,578 CpG markers of which 406,807 were retained after quality-control filtering. A continuous feature-ranking framework merging Random Forest importance and ANOVA F-statistics was applied across repeated runs. Biological relevance was evaluated through hypergeometric enrichment against a curated PDAC gene set and preranked Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using 309 Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways. All seven analysis strategies produced significant enrichment for literature-supported pancreatic cancer-associated genes, with hypergeometric p-values ranging from 3.34&times;10&minus;16 to 1.28&times;10&minus;7. SMOTE recovered the largest absolute number of PDAC-associated genes (141 of 13,827 selected genes), whereas RUS achieved the greatest fold enrichment (2.17-fold; 88 observed versus 40.61 expected). Notably, the no-resampling baseline remained highly competitive, recovering 112 PDAC-associated genes with 1.86-fold enrichment and a p-value of 5.27&times;10&minus;14, indicating that resampling was not necessary to recover biologically relevant features under the evaluated feature-ranking framework. Across methods, 169&ndash;234 of the 309 tested KEGG pathways were significant at false discovery rate &le;0.05. ClusterCentroids produced the largest number of significant pathways (234), followed by the no-resampling baseline (225) and RUS (223). Seven to nine predefined PDAC-focused pathways were recovered per method, with RUS and ClusterCentroids recovering all nine. Core pathways consistently identified across all methods included MAPK, PI3K&ndash;Akt, TGF-&beta;, Notch, Hedgehog, focal adhesion, and cell-cycle signaling. These findings show that resampling strategies produce distinct trade-offs between biomarker coverage, biological specificity, and pathway breadth, supporting biologically informed evaluation rather than selection of a single universally optimal imbalance-correction method.

title: DP-FDT: The Drug Pair-Based Fuzzy Decision Tree for Accurate Drug Combination Prediction
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm, the Drug Pair-based Fuzzy Decision Tree (DP-FDT), designed to improve classification performance on imbalanced drug combination datasets. Unlike traditional decision trees, the DP-FDT integrates drug combination feature pairs into its feature selection and node construction processes to better capture the underlying relationships between features from different drugs. The algorithm employs a fuzzy splitting rule that allows samples to be assigned to both child nodes with certain probabilities, thereby enhancing the model&rsquo;s fault tolerance. In addition, logistic regression classifiers are incorporated at impure leaf nodes to provide an additional means of separating samples that cannot be perfectly partitioned. Experimental results on two cell line datasets (A375 and A549) demonstrate that the DP-FDT achieves superior performance, particularly in terms of AUC and F1 score, compared with several state-of-the-art oblique decision trees and a deep learning baseline. It also improves recall for minority classes. Ablation studies confirm the positive contributions of its key components. Furthermore, a preliminary bioinformatics analysis provides insights into the biological processes associated with the most influential features identified by the model. Overall, the DP-FDT offers an effective and interpretable approach for analyzing complex drug combination data.

title: AI-Generated Text Detection via Structural and Semantic Entropy Optimization with Adversarial Learning
abstract: AI-generated text detectors often achieve high in-domain accuracy but remain sensitive to changes in domain, generator, and writing style. This limitation partly arises because conventional detectors rely predominantly on latent language-model representations and fixed decision boundaries, without explicitly characterizing sample-level structural and semantic variation. We introduce S2E-AL, an end-to-end score-aware structure&ndash;semantic entropy adversarial learning framework for AI-generated text detection. S2E-AL encodes local dependency, global contextual, and semantic entropy features into a structure&ndash;semantic representation. A gradient-reversal source classifier discourages this representation from retaining source-specific information, while a score-aware threshold estimator conditions on both the entropy representation and a detached base-detector logit to produce a sample-specific logit adjustment. The adjusted logit is used to estimate the final probability that a text is AI-generated. Across HC3, HC3_Plus, LLMTrace, RAID, and XSum, the score-aware model achieved a macro Accuracy of 90.90% and a macro F1-score of 91.42%. Its performance remained lower on XSum, indicating that substantial domain and stylistic shifts remain challenging. These results suggest that jointly modeling structure&ndash;semantic variation and detector confidence can improve the overall performance&ndash;stability trade-off of AI-generated text detection across heterogeneous test distributions.

title: Stream Reduction in Multi-Stream Graph Convolutional Networks: A Non-Inferiority Study for Skeleton-Based Action Recognition
abstract: Multi-stream graph convolutional networks improve skeleton action recognition by combining representations, but each branch adds inference cost. We evaluate one fixed stream-removal operating point in a CTR-GCN pipeline using a paired non-inferiority protocol on NTU RGB+D 120. A temporal configuration reduced source-frame entries requested from the skeleton store by 53.52%, but lost 3.191 percentage points of accuracy and provided no latency saving after reopening the data mapping. A three-stream configuration then omitted bone motion while retaining 64 temporal positions. Historical RTX 4090 measurements at batch size one, using development checkpoints, showed 24.30&ndash;24.94% lower latency. After development confirmation, the fixed pair was trained on 54,468 examples and evaluated on 59,477 cross-setup test examples. Overall accuracy was 89.1050% for four streams and 89.0277% for three streams; paired setup-bootstrap lower bounds exceeded all three prespecified non-inferiority margins. Stream removal introduced 605 errors and corrected 559, while predicted labels changed for 1778 examples. Thus, a net loss of 46 correct decisions concealed broader redistribution. Recall decreased for 61 of 120 actions. These findings support assessing a branch by its contribution to the complete system, measured cost, and explicit quality tolerances. They do not imply preservation of every action. A separate CPU experiment with the final checkpoints measured 24.67% mean latency saving across three processes on one host. The contribution is a controlled empirical assessment, not a new architecture.

title: Generative AI Literacy and Multidimensional AI Anxiety in Creative Higher Education
abstract: Engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involves practical literacy as well as learning, professional, sociotechnical, and configuration concerns. This mixed-methods study examined whether these responses were differentiated among Chinese arts-university students. Primary inference used a quality-screened cross-sectional sample of 355 questionnaire records from 351 participant-identifier clusters after excluding 105 of 460 eligible records (22.8%) showing exact whole-battery straightlining across all 59 structured items; the full eligible sample of 460 records from 455 clusters was retained as a sensitivity analysis. GenAI literacy was assessed with a 16-item music-context-adapted self-report instrument covering cognitive (CL), behavioral (BL), affective (AL), and ethical (EL) literacy, and AI Anxiety with 21 items spanning Learning Anxiety (LA), Job-Replacement Anxiety (JR), Sociotechnical Blindness Anxiety (ST), and AI Configuration Anxiety (AC). Of six prespecified associations, only EL-JR and EL-ST met the Holm-adjusted criterion in the primary sample and remained supported in the full-sample and prior-use-adjusted sensitivity analyses. CL-LA and BL-LA were unsupported in both samples, whereas AL-LA and AL-AC were sample-specification sensitive. Measurement models showed mixed fit; CL-BL separation improved after quality screening but remained incomplete. A secondary 47-person exact-identifier matched panel showed higher later-wave CL, BL, and AL scores, whereas EL and all four AI Anxiety dimensions showed no Holm-adjusted difference. These literacy comparisons are exploratory because the administered literacy items were music-framed while the documented learning activities involved broadcasting scripts and AI-supported video production. Independently analyzed qualitative material provided construct-level consistency with the EL-ST interpretation and tentative complementarity for EL-JR, but was not participant-linked to the quantitative samples. Overall, the evidence supports a bounded interpretation of differentiated, calibrated rather than anxiety-free adaptation; it does not establish causal intervention effects or participant-level mixed-method mechanisms.

title: Understanding Regression in Code Self-Refinement: A Study of Refinement Protocols Without Execution Feedback
abstract: Self-refinement can improve generated code without additional training, but without execution feedback, revision can also turn already correct code into incorrect code. We study how self-refinement protocol design affects code correctness using six locally deployable open-weight models, three Python code-generation benchmarks, and 9984 model-task pairs. Using the same initial code for each protocol, we compare direct revision with refinement that adds critique and planning, test whether asking the model if revision is needed before refining affects correctness, and compare separate calls with a single response. Among the evaluated refinement protocols, direct revision achieved the highest overall correctness, whereas adding separate Critique and Planning stages increased repairs but caused substantially more regressions. Direct revision produced 55 repairs and 20 regressions; adding Critique produced 220 repairs and 605 regressions, and adding Planning after Critique produced 206 repairs and 719 regressions. Decision filtering and Single-call organization improved the regression-prone protocols by reducing harmful changes. They improved pass rate by 3.89 to 5.10 and 3.22 to 3.92 percentage points, respectively, but neither approach surpassed direct revision. Repeated direct generation produced many repairs simply by generating another candidate, while direct revision maintained a much more favorable repair-regression balance. These results suggest that, without execution feedback, refinement designs should prioritize preserving already correct code over adding reasoning stages.

title: FedQDFU: Non-IID Federated Quantum Learning for Diabetic Foot Ulcer Classification from Deep Image Features
abstract: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) classification increasingly relies on learning frameworks that exploit medical image representations without centralizing raw data. This study presents FedQDFU, a feature-based federated quantum learning benchmark evaluating a compact variational quantum classifier (VQC) on deep features from VGG16, ResNet50, and DenseNet121, using frozen ImageNet-pretrained backbones as fixed feature extractors over 1020 samples from a single public DFU dataset (696 unique feature vectors after exact-duplicate auditing). Because patient identifiers are unavailable, duplicate-group-aware splitting prevents exact duplicates from crossing the development-test boundary but cannot guarantee patient-level independence. A 6-qubit VQC (43 parameters) is compared with a 129-parameter multilayer perceptron (MLP) under centralized learning, FedAvg, and FedProx across IID and Dirichlet non-IID client distributions (&alpha;&isin;{10,1,0.5,0.1}), with federated-compatible random projection, five-seed evaluation of the primary conditions, and bootstrap confidence intervals on a locked test set. At the primary non-IID setting (&alpha;=0.5), the VQC attains a lower mean Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) than the MLP on all three backbones (e.g., ResNet50: 0.782&plusmn;0.011 vs. 0.650&plusmn;0.041 under FedAvg); the paired bootstrap difference is significant only for ResNet50 at the uncorrected pairwise 95% level (&Delta;MCC=&minus;0.115, 95% CI [&minus;0.218,&minus;0.016]), an effect a Bonferroni correction across backbones is estimated to remove, so this result should be read as suggestive rather than confirmed. No significant centralized-to-FedAvg VQC degradation is detected for any backbone, and a ResNet50 parameter-matched experiment shows the MLP-VQC gap persists even when the MLP is reduced to 41 parameters. Under severe non-IID heterogeneity (&alpha;=0.1), the seed-42 partition contains one entirely single-class client (mean pairwise Jensen&ndash;Shannon divergence 0.5653 vs. 0.1787 at &alpha;=0.5); federated aggregation of this degenerate update yields a fixed-threshold collapse in which all test samples are assigned the positive class (MCC = 0, sensitivity = 1, specificity = 0). This outcome is realization-dependent rather than deterministic: only one of five paired partition/training seeds reproduces the complete collapse.

title: Explicit Multi-Scale Feature Learning Through a Human Visual System-Inspired Coarse&ndash;Medium&ndash;Fine Network for Maize Leaf Disease Classification
abstract: Accurately recognizing maize leaf diseases requires analyzing visual information expressed across multiple spatial scales. This includes the leaf&rsquo;s overall appearance, intermediate-scale texture structures, and localized lesion patterns. This study proposes a coarse&ndash;medium&ndash;fine (CMF) architecture inspired by the human visual system that uses a convolutional neural network to classify maize leaf images into four categories: blight, common rust, gray leaf spot, and healthy. The CMF architecture contains three parallel convolutional branches that learn complementary coarse, medium, and fine representations. The feature maps are integrated through a weighted fusion strategy and processed by a fully connected classifier. The model was trained from scratch using a balanced subset of 2000 original images selected from the Corn or Maize Leaf Disease Dataset. The experimental protocol used 1600 images for training and 400 for testing. Augmentation was applied to the training set only; the testing set remained unchanged. The Coarse, Medium, and Fine branches achieved accuracies of 87.95&plusmn;0.58, 89.85&plusmn;0.51, and 95.10&plusmn;0.39, respectively. A fixed held-out test partition was used to evaluate the three individual branches and the complete CMF model. Five balanced random subsets of 300 images (75 images per class) were employed for this evaluation. The resulting performance was summarized using the mean and standard deviation across the five test-subset evaluations. The complete CMF model achieved 99.25&plusmn;0.27 accuracy, as well as macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score values of 99.27&plusmn;0.26, 99.25&plusmn;0.27, and 99.24&plusmn;0.26, respectively. Under a common, repeated, random subsampling evaluation protocol applied to the three individual branches and the complete CMF model, the fused model improved accuracy by 4.15 percentage points relative to the Fine branch. Blight and Healthy achieved recall values of 100.00&plusmn;0.00, while Gray Leaf Spot and Common Rust achieved recall values of 99.00&plusmn;0.15% and 98&plusmn;0.39%, respectively. The branch-level and fused-model results support the complementary role of the three spatial representations under the evaluated experimental conditions. The proposed CMF architecture provides an explicit, multiscale learning framework for image-based maize leaf disease classification and motivates further evaluation under practical agricultural conditions.

title: When Deployment Changes a Learned Action: Post-Inference Projection in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Learned control is commonly evaluated at the policy output, although a deployment layer may transform that output before execution. We study this post-inference semantic boundary for offline multi-agent reinforcement learning policies that produce three-component simplex actions. Training and model weights are held fixed; at deployment, an action is either preserved or projected to the one-hot vector of its largest component. The intervention is evaluated in programmable multipath network control using three network structures, two policy architectures, and ten matched model&ndash;traffic replications. The resulting 120 deployment episodes form 60 policy-level contrasts and 30 shared topology&ndash;traffic blocks. Preserving the continuous action favored the end-host successful-session fraction and the controller-side path-sum utilization in all 60 contrasts and externally measured traffic loss in 59; reward, bottleneck utilization, receiver throughput, and controller-probe latency were less uniform. The ten pairs are the independent replication unit, with topology and architecture as crossed conditions; all ten favored preservation for every outcome, a two-sided sign-test probability of 0.002 under an equal-sign reference model. Mean favorable differences were 0.540 percentage points in external loss, 0.00539 in successful-session fraction, and 0.0416 in reward. Two supplementary online arms sharpen the interpretation: top-2 renormalization recovered most of the argmax deficit, whereas a separately trained discrete learner was outperformed even by the projected policy, so the deficit is not merely training&ndash;deployment mismatch. Continuous actions remained materially fractional, with mean discarded mass under argmax between approximately 0.45 and 0.53, but action geometry showed no measurable association with the size of the deployment effect. Argmax therefore removes substantial action structure and the two deployment interpretations produce different system behavior, without discarded mass being identified as the causal mediator. Deployment-aware evaluation should report both the policy output and the executable interpretation applied after inference.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Large Language Models in the Analysis of Linear Electrical Circuits
abstract: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence systems has massively expanded the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) even in complex engineering domains, where formal accuracy and logical-mathematical consistency are essential requirements. This study analyzes the issue of the reliability of large language models in the analytical solution of linear electrical circuits; the main objective is to conduct a comparative evaluation of four high-end, reasoning-oriented LLMs (ChatGPT 5.6 Luna, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash, and Microsoft Copilot GPT-4o) in order to examine their accuracy, logical and mathematical consistency, and robustness in the analysis of electrical networks under different operating conditions. A structured benchmark of 90 original circuit-analysis problems was developed, equally distributed across DC steady-state, transient, and sinusoidal AC circuits and stratified into Easy, Medium, and Hard difficulty levels. Each problem contained two analytical questions and was independently submitted to each model three times, resulting in 2160 individually evaluated answers. Circuits were provided as SPICE-compatible textual netlists with task annotations, and reference solutions were analytically derived and validated using SPICE. Overall question-level accuracy was 92.2% for Claude, 53.9% for ChatGPT, 51.3% for Gemini, and 33.1% for Copilot. A binomial generalized linear mixed model revealed significant effects of model, circuit domain, and difficulty, together with significant Model &times; Domain and Model &times; Difficulty interactions, whereas no systematic effect of run was detected. Run-to-run analysis nevertheless revealed substantial differences in score consistency among models. The findings show that LLM performance in circuit analysis is strongly model-, domain-, and difficulty-dependent and that repeated outputs may remain unstable even when no systematic run effect is present. The proposed benchmark provides a reproducible framework for assessing the capabilities and limitations of LLMs in structured engineering problem solving.

title: Reliable Learning-Enabled Multi-Robot Coverage with Masked Entity-Attention MAPPO: A Controlled Multi-Seed Study
abstract: Learning-enabled control requires training to produce competent policies consistently when success requires every robot to finish. This study evaluates masked entity-attention multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) for simulated landmark coverage by five differential-drive robots. Configurations were compared under a fixed reward, optimizer, stopping rule, and 100 held-out scenarios, using trained seeds as statistical units; the actor observes the robot&ndash;landmark scene but not the externally computed assignment. Across ten policies per principal configuration, masked entity attention achieved 94.6&plusmn;4.7% deterministic full-team success, against 9.3&plusmn;12.4% and 6.8&plusmn;5.1% for wider (1.21 times its parameters) and ordinary fixed-index controls, every masked-attention seed exceeding every seed of both fixed-index controls. Near-parameter-matched Deep Sets and unmasked-attention controls reached 73.7&plusmn;14.0% and 72.1&plusmn;13.1%, overlapping it. The same policies retained 91.4&ndash;96.3% mean success from three to eight robots without retraining, and masked attention remained separated from both fixed-index controls at every rate in a 45-policy learning-rate design. Held-out scenes come from the training distribution; under shift, success fell to 70.9% in an unseen larger workspace, while landmark, sensing, and actuation perturbations kept it above 93.3%. Masked entity-attention MAPPO gives the most consistent full-team completion among the tested designs; broader robustness and physical deployment remain unestablished.

title: Agentic AI in Construction: A Systematic Review and Human-Governed Framework for Autonomous Project Delivery
abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) has emerged as a new paradigm that extends conventional artificial intelligence by integrating autonomous reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and adaptive decision-making into goal-directed systems. Although interest in Agentic AI has rapidly increased, its application within the construction industry remains fragmented and lacks a comprehensive synthesis. This study presents a systematic literature review of Agentic AI in construction, following the PRISMA methodology and analysing 50 journal articles published between 2021 and 2026. The review examines the conceptual evolution of Agentic AI, architectural paradigms, intelligence mechanisms, enabling technologies, lifecycle applications, reported benefits, validation approaches, adoption barriers, and future research directions. The findings show a clear transition from precursor forms of computational agency, including rule-based agent-based modelling and reinforcement-learning systems, towards contemporary Agentic AI characterised by increasingly modular, hybrid, tool-enabled, multi-agent, and human-governed architectures supported by large language models, digital twins, robotics, and Internet of Things technologies. Current applications primarily support project planning, scheduling, logistics, safety management, inspection, quality control, structural design, and facility operation. However, most studies remain at prototype or simulation stages, with limited real-world deployment and inconsistent evaluation methods. The review also identifies significant technical, organisational, and governance challenges, including engineering reliability, interoperability, explainability, human oversight, and data integration. Building on these findings, the study proposes the Human-Governed Construction Agentic Intelligence Loop (H-CAIL), a construction-specific closed-loop framework that integrates project context, multimodal perception, goal-directed planning, reasoning, tool selection, human-governed action, evaluation, and adaptive learning to support trustworthy autonomous decision-making across the construction lifecycle. Finally, the study presents a future research agenda to support the development of trustworthy, scalable, and construction-specific Agentic AI ecosystems capable of enabling autonomous yet human-governed project delivery across the entire asset lifecycle.

title: Evaluating Safety Embedding Prefiltering for Analyzing Millions of LLM Agent Social Network Messages for Security and Safety Harms
abstract: Agentic social networks expose autonomous agents to large volumes of potentially malicious content, including prompt injection, social engineering, and unsafe execution requests. Large Language Model (LLM) judges can detect such content, but applying them at platform scale is expensive. We study the extent to which lightweight embedding-based prefilters can reduce this cost while retaining most of the judge&rsquo;s unsafe predictions. We annotate 10,000 Moltbook posts and comments with a frontier LLM judge, assigning a binary safety verdict, severity level, malicious intent taxonomy labels, and Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) AI risk codes. Of the LLM-annotated samples, 9.2% were unsafe at severity 3 or above. Two human annotators with high inter-rater agreement (Cohen&rsquo;s &kappa;=0.823) exhibited moderate agreement between their adjudicated labels and the LLM ratings (&kappa;=0.578). We compare centroid-based cosine prefilters over 3 off-the-shelf encoders against a supervised trained classifier. Reducing the input window size raises average precision by up to 6.3 percentage points. At an operating point calibrated to 0.80 recall, the projected cost of scanning 787,226 messages falls from $7085 by 49.9% (MiniLM-L12-v2), 55.6% (BGE-M3), and 65.6% (trained classifier), while MiniLM runs roughly 32 times faster than the classifier. Prefiltering can therefore make frontier-judge screening affordable at scale, although jailbreak content remains the hardest category to retrieve.

title: A Cache-Aware Compression Framework: Deriving the Compression Target and Stopping Rule for Transformers on CPU-Class Hardware
abstract: In post-training compression of Transformer models, the compression ratio or pruning rate is often predetermined and does not directly take into account the memory capabilities of the target hardware. This work introduces a cache-aware post-training compression framework for CPU-class hardware. The framework derives the minimum required compression ratio from the effective weight working set of the operator or layer and the effective level-3 (L3) cache budget. The cache budget is treated as a hardware resource shared with concurrent modules rather than as a latency heuristic. If functional redundancy is present, functionally similar channels are physically removed using compensated structured pruning; in cases where final 8-bit integer (INT8) alone cannot meet the hardware target, activation-aware low-rank factorization is used. The resulting weights are quantized to per-output-channel INT8 using GPTQ, and the final configuration is evaluated by a task-level accuracy gate. In the Whisper-medium Uzbek automatic speech recognition (ASR) encoder, removing 17.1% of the feed-forward network (FFN) channels reduced the size from 300 MiB to 267 MiB, with the word error rate (WER) difference from the GPTQ-only variant (per-output-channel INT8 without structured pruning) not statistically distinguishable (&Delta;WER = &minus;0.0014, 95% confidence interval (CI) [&minus;0.0115, +0.0096]). For the full model, the cascade achieved 4.14&times; compression at 705 MiB with WER = 0.1833, whereas extending compression to 5.34&times; increased WER to 0.6101. Hardware profiling showed 2.41&times; fewer memory stalls and a 1.91&times; reduction in encoder-plus-decoder-step execution time. End-to-end response time improved by 2.36&times;, reducing the real audio RTF from 2.57 to 1.09. Taken together, these results support hardware-derived targeting with accuracy-guided stopping as an alternative to selecting a fixed compression ratio in advance.

title: CognitiveCPQ: A Graph-Based Reinforcement Learning Framework for Autonomous Constraint-Aware Enterprise Deal Optimisation
abstract: Configure-Price-Quote (CPQ) systems are central to enterprise B2B sales execution, yet most deployments remain rule-based and deterministic, unable to learn from deal outcomes. This paper presents CognitiveCPQ, combining a Heterogeneous Constraint Graph (HCG) with Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) for autonomous, constraint-aware deal optimisation. A deterministic kill-switch guarantees zero hard constraint violations; soft constraints are navigated via a z-score-normalised penalised reward. A KernelSHAP explainability layer provides per-decision attribution. Evaluation on a large-scale synthetic simulation demonstrates 18.9% margin uplift, 94.3% constraint compliance, and a 67% reduction in configuration steps over rule-based baselines. We additionally specify two robustness evaluation protocols&mdash;response-model misspecification and state-observability noise&mdash;as immediate follow-up work; both protocols are expected to confirm graceful degradation given the kill-switch&rsquo;s structural independence from the response model and state vector. All results represent proof-of-concept performance in simulation; production deployment requires shadow-mode calibration on real deal data.

title: Anti-Jamming Algorithm Based on Stackelberg Game and Soft Actor-Critic
abstract: This paper studies a hybrid anti-jamming architecture using a Stackelberg game as its theoretical formulation in which a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent selects a robustness radius and a power-control coefficient, while model-based power allocation and second-order cone programming determine transmit powers and receive-combining weights. The experimental evaluation uses a frequency-selective multipath Rician channel with diffuse scattering, path delays, and Doppler evolution. Three training runs are assessed using deterministic policies on fixed control channels and a separate test set. On the separate test, training increases mean reward from 4.133 to 14.483 and reduces average-SINR outage at 12 dB from 0.935 to 0.403, accompanied by an increase in normalized transmit power from 0.690 to 0.979. An independently tuned fixed-parameter baseline achieves reward 14.923 and outage 0.374. The results demonstrate improvement over the initial policy, but do not establish an advantage over tuned fixed parameters. Robust feasibility remains conditional on the channel-uncertainty set and numerical feasibility; the simulated jammer uses an exogenous allocation rule, so the experiments do not verify a Stackelberg equilibrium.

title: Integrating Sentiment Analysis and Intuitionistic Fuzzy Set for Large-Scale Decision-Making
abstract: Traditional group decision-making methods are typically employed with a limited number of experts and alternatives. Nevertheless, in real-world scenarios, such as those involving social networks or e-democracy in municipalities or companies, these methods face limitations due to the involvement of many experts and the vast amount of generated information. In addressing this challenge, Large-Scale Group Decision-Making methods have been developed. Nonetheless, enhancements remain needed to leverage the wealth of available information fully. For example, expert comments during debates are often overlooked. We have devised an innovative approach to tackle this issue and effectively manage the information provided by experts. Our method facilitates expert debates where preferences, both positive and negative, are expressed, and leverages this input to derive neutral information through intuitionistic fuzzy sets, thereby enhancing the decision-making process. Furthermore, employing sentiment analysis, our method categorizes comments as positive, negative, or neutral. By integrating expert insights, sentiment analysis results, and a newly developed aggregation operator, we consolidate information, enabling the calculation of a comprehensive ranking that accounts for the abundance of available data.

title: SISAD: Semantic Interference Suppression for Multimodal Time-Series Anomaly Detection
abstract: Multimodal time-series anomaly detection incorporates textual data regarding external events to provide contextual information for numerical fluctuations; this facilitates the interpretation of sudden fluctuations in complex systems&mdash;such as those caused by disasters, public events, or environmental changes&mdash;and enables the identification of numerical fluctuations that cannot be explained by the available context. However, existing methods typically treat text as an auxiliary feature for enhancement while still relying primarily on the degree of deviation in numerical sequences to detect anomalies; consequently, they struggle to distinguish between explainable fluctuations driven by genuine external events and fluctuations that are unsupported by the available event semantics. Moreover, redundant, mismatched, or weakly correlated text can disrupt the modeling of normal temporal patterns, potentially triggering cross-modal negative transfer. To address these issues, we propose SISAD, a multimodal time-series anomaly-detection method based on semantic interference suppression. First, the method employs trend decoupling and multiscale encoding to extract local temporal variation patterns, thereby mitigating the impact of low-frequency trends on the modeling of localized or fine-grained temporal variations. Second, it constructs a prototype-based semantic fusion module that integrates external event text, endogenous statistical text, and domain prior knowledge, enhancing the semantic interpretability of the current segment by retrieving learned historical prototypes. Finally, a semantic interference suppression module is designed to measure the degree of cross-modal conflict and adaptively adjust the text fusion intensity; this allows relevant text to contribute to reconstruction and discrimination while attenuating interference from unreliable text.&nbsp;Experiments conducted on seven datasets spanning three domains demonstrate that SISAD outperforms existing methods across most datasets and key metrics, showing improved performance in distinguishing fluctuations with relevant contextual support from those that cannot be explained by the available context.&nbsp;Ablation and text-perturbation experiments further support the contributions of prototype-based semantic fusion and semantic interference suppression with the evaluated settings.

title: Multimodal LLM Pipeline for Automated Analysis of Technical Graphical Documents
abstract: Automating the evaluation of technical documents, such as laboratory reports, requires balancing accurate multimodal information extraction with efficient downstream processing. This paper proposes a vision&ndash;language model (VLM) processing pipeline that extracts textual and graphical content into structured intermediate representations (JSON), enabling subsequent document assessment without redundant image retransmission. We evaluate the approach across a corpus of laboratory reports, investigating the impact of prompting strategies on text extraction and document analysis. The evaluation reveals distinct performance trade-offs across prompting configurations: Prompt 10 with Llama 4 Maverick achieved the highest textual overlap (Dice = 0.7402), whereas Prompt 5 yielded the highest observed TF-IDF cosine similarity and normalized Levenshtein similarity scores. Furthermore, downstream validation using structured text representations provides a viable architectural approach to avoid repeated visual-input transmission in multi-stage analysis workflows. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of structured intermediate representations for technical document parsing, while highlighting how specific prompt designs trade off different extraction quality metrics.

title: Dynamic Inference Techniques in Convolutional Neural Networks: A Review
abstract: The demand for more accurate Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has led to increasingly deep and computationally expensive models. These architectures face limiting deployment and resource constraints when implemented. Static CNN models treat all input samples with identical computational density. These models are inefficient given the variability of real-world data. Dynamic inference solutions focus on this challenge by presenting computational graphs on a per-input basis. This allows considerable optimization of the efficiency&ndash;accuracy trade-off. This review offers a structured synthesis of dynamic inference solutions in CNNs, distributed over three architectural dimensions: depth, width, and spatial resolution. For each aspect, we present representative models, alongside their training strategies, and examine their practical constraints and performance trade-offs. We further present multi-dimensional hybrid architectures based on combining these aspects for accumulated efficiency gains. By critically analyzing each approach and their challenges&mdash;including hardware limitations, training instability, and constrained deployment scope&mdash;this paper offers a roadmap for future work in optimized deep learning modelling.

title: TCAV-Based Cross-Representation Explainability for Facial Emotion Recognition
abstract: Deep learning has achieved strong predictive performance in facial emotion recognition (FER), but interpreting the internal representations underlying model decisions remains challenging. In this study, we propose a cross-representation concept-based explainability framework that extends TCAV analysis beyond a single visual representation by evaluating the same human-interpretable facial concepts in both latent image features and explicit landmark-derived geometric features. AffectNet and CK+ facial image databases were analyzed using a frozen pretrained EmoNet backbone with a task-specific classification head, and landmark-derived geometric features were classified with FLAML AutoML. We analyzed seven human-interpretable concepts, such as mouth width, mouth opening, bilateral eye openness, bilateral eyebrow raising, and facial asymmetry, through visual TCAV and P25/P75-based tabular TCAV. The image-based model outperforms the geometric model, with reported accuracies of 0.7111 and 0.9329 on AffectNet and CK+, respectively, versus 0.6640 and 0.8265 on tabular data. TCAV found strong concept&ndash;emotion relationships, but they depended on the concept representation. Visual concepts tended to have stronger sensitivities, while geometric concepts had more moderate relationships that were directly interpretable. Visual and geometric representations provide complementary explanations for FER decisions. Concept stability, dataset dependence, and concept-class confounding are still important considerations for reliable TCAV interpretation.

title: Trustworthy Multimodal Tool-Wear Prediction: Bias Auditing, Lifecycle Mitigation, and the Data-Adequacy Limits of Algorithmic Correction
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for tool-wear prediction in computer numerical control (CNC) machining, yet a high average accuracy can conceal systematic failure in the safety-critical high-wear region, where under-prediction makes a worn tool appear healthier than it is. This paper presents a trustworthy multimodal framework that audits, mitigates, and ultimately characterises this bias on the public MATWI dataset. A fusion model combining 512 image features with 84 force, acceleration, and acoustic features attains a strong test mean absolute error (MAE) of 30.9&mu;m, outperforming image-only (51.4&mu;m) and sensor-only (68.3&mu;m) baselines. A signed, stratified bias audit nevertheless reveals a pronounced directional error: the model predicts the healthy region to within 21.3&mu;m but under-predicts the worn region by approximately 85&mu;m (worn-region MAE 85.5&mu;m), with the error deepening monotonically as wear increases. A three-stage mitigation pipeline&mdash;data-level resampling, cost-sensitive and relevance-based training, and post-hoc recalibration&mdash;reduces the worn-region error by 18% for the combined pipeline and by up to 22% for the best single-stage configuration, but cannot eliminate it, and only at a measurable cost to the well-sampled region. The residual bias persists across six regressor families sharing the same fused representation, with a 69&ndash;127&mu;m residual gap, and survives rigorous hyperparameter search and bias-aware loss functions behind an &asymp;85&mu;m error floor. At every maintenance threshold evaluated the model produces a 100% false-safe rate.Under the feature representation and sampling of this dataset, the bias is therefore not addressable by model family, mitigation strategy, or optimisation, which identifies data adequacy rather than model design as the binding constraint. The conclusion is scoped accordingly: alternative feature representations, generative augmentation, and domain adaptation were not evaluated and remain open. The contribution is a reusable protocol for distinguishing model-reducible from data-limited bias in safety-critical regression.

title: Performance of Stateful Hash-Based PQ-Digital Signatures in Industrial Scenarios
abstract: Quantum computers endanger the security of digital signatures as they are generated today, e.g., by cryptographic algorithms like RSA, DSA, and ECDSA, whose security is based on algebraic problems. They have to be replaced by quantum-computer-resistant algorithms, so-called PQ (post-quantum) cryptography. This paper describes the performance results of one type of PQ digital signature embedded in the OPC UA communication protocol, measured in a typical industrial environment, demonstrating the communication between a sensor or actuator and an operator over a 5G campus network. The PQ digital signatures tested follow the stateful hash-based digital signature algorithm (SFH-DSA) as defined by ISO/IEC 14888-4. The tests show that this example of quantum-computer-resistant cryptographic algorithms is useful for practical use cases in industrial applications, which are characterized by real-time requirements and reliable communication between electronic components. Computation times, transmission times including overhead, lengths of digital signatures, memory requirements, and other characteristics are measured for different security levels and different types of hardware. These PQ-resistant digital signatures show very good performance properties, which make them useful for future industrial applications.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical and Surgical Information: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Readability, Reliability, and Emotional Resonance
abstract: Background: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized for patient-facing healthcare communication. However, their clinical utility remains constrained by communicative, ethical, and safety challenges. This systematic review provides a cross-specialty evaluation of conversational AI, synthesizing evidence on accuracy, readability, informational quality, and emotional resonance. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and PROSPERO registration (CRD420251021428), PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched from 2020 through November 2025. Eligible studies evaluated LLM-generated medical or surgical information against healthcare professionals, validated benchmarks, or alternative AI platforms. Assessed outcomes included factual accuracy, standardized readability indices (e.g., FKGL, FRES), validated quality metrics (e.g., DISCERN, GQS), and emotional or empathetic impact. Results: Eighty-two studies (published 2023&ndash;2025) were included. Accuracy was evaluated in 45 studies, demonstrating generally high performance (mean Likert scores &gt; 3.5/5); advanced GPT models frequently showed parity or superiority to comparators, though factual errors persisted in complex clinical reasoning. Readability, assessed in 69 studies, emerged as the primary limitation: baseline outputs consistently required high school or university-level comprehension (FKGL &gt; 10&ndash;12), substantially exceeding recommended patient literacy thresholds (&le;8th grade). Informational quality, appraised in 35 studies, was rated moderate-to-high across DISCERN and GQS metrics. Six studies evaluating emotional resonance indicated that LLMs can alleviate situational anxiety and deliver structured cognitive empathy comparable or superior to brief clinician text, though lacking genuine emotional depth. Conclusions: LLMs demonstrate strong factual accuracy and structural quality across diverse clinical disciplines. However, autonomous, patient-facing deployment remains premature due to excessive lexical density that threatens health equity. Conversational AI should function as a clinical adjunct to support providers rather than an unsupervised educational tool. Future research must prioritize dynamic literacy alignment and robust clinical validation.

title: A Layered Decision-Aware Forecasting Architecture for Noisy Panel Environments
abstract: Machine learning forecasting systems in noisy, non-stationary, multi-entity environments are commonly optimized for pointwise predictive accuracy, although many downstream decisions depend on the relative ordering of entities rather than exact numerical forecasts. This creates a potential prediction&ndash;ranking&ndash;decision misalignment, where the model with the lowest forecast error may not generate the most useful ranking or decision outcome. This paper proposes a Layered Decision-Aware Forecasting Architecture (LDFA) that separates predictive calibration from decision-oriented transformation. Layers 1 and 2 generate heterogeneous forecasts through base learners, stacking, and adaptive weighting, while the main methodological contribution is Layer 3: a selective post-prediction controller based on source selection, activation gating, veto logic, and regime-aware scaling. LDFA is evaluated using daily data for 30 EGX firms from 2020 to 2025 under a leakage-controlled expanding-window walk-forward protocol. The results show that prediction, ranking, and decision metrics favor different models: the Ridge meta-model provides the strongest target-scale accuracy, the XGBRankerLTR learning-to-rank baseline achieves the strongest ranking information coefficient (IC), and the SoftmaxHybridGate achieves the highest Sharpe ratio. The Layer 3 controller slightly improves over the Ridge backbone in mean daily IC, Sharpe ratio, and maximum drawdown, but the gains are modest and not statistically conclusive. Ablation and sensitivity analyses show that uncontrolled correction is harmful, while selective activation is the main value-adding mechanism. Transaction-cost, dynamic-controller, bootstrap, and top-k robustness tests further indicate that LDFA is most useful under selective decision settings rather than as a universally dominant model. The findings position LDFA as a transparent decision-aware forecasting architecture for studying and managing prediction&ndash;ranking&ndash;decision trade-offs in noisy panel environments.

title: Scored Rule Sets: A Unified Framework for Interpretable Classification, Regression, and Cluster Explanation
abstract: Interpretable machine learning on tabular data has traditionally relied on fragmented rule-induction ecosystems, where distinct paradigms are used for discrete and continuous targets, and transparent post hoc explanation of unsupervised structures is rarely integrated under a single model class. This article presents a unified, task-aware formalization of the scored-rule-set framework that spans multiclass classification, continuous regression, and transparent cluster explanation while preserving logical comprehensibility and modularity as primary design goals. By establishing an explicit task-aware formalization R=(S,&tau;,G&tau;) that decouples rule-condition discovery from task-specific score-vector semantics and commutative aggregation operators, we consolidate foundations established in prior classification research, introduce a native regression runtime with scikit-learn compatibility, and formulate a two-stage surrogate pipeline for explaining arbitrary clustering assignments via transparent rule sets. Across extensive empirical evaluations on standard tabular benchmarks, we compare predictive performance, explanation fidelity, and model simplicity across heuristic, genetic programming, and multi-objective evolutionary backends. The results demonstrate that task-aware scored rule sets achieve competitive accuracy across both supervised regimes and high explanation fidelity in unsupervised settings, establishing scored rule sets as a versatile, holistic foundation for transparent tabular machine learning.

title: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for LLM-Driven Task Planning and Execution in Industrial Assembly
abstract: This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic framework that combines large language model (LLM)-driven task planning with formal symbolic verification and reactive Behavior Tree execution to support high-precision operations in industrial assembly. While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate expertise in interpreting natural language instructions, they often struggle with processing structured manufacturing data and lack long-horizon planning capabilities and deterministic physical awareness required for complex robotic execution. Furthermore, their susceptibility to generating physically unfeasible sequences and their lack of robust error-recovery mechanisms limit their autonomous deployment. To address these limitations, the proposed pipeline decomposes the assembly process into sequential stages of planning, technological grounding, adaptive execution, and recovery. Initially, the framework leverages LLMs to synthesize multi-modal inputs&mdash;ranging from natural language directives to formalized product and process specifications&mdash;into a formal Hierarchical Task Network (HTN). To ensure physical feasibility, a deterministic rule-based compiler validates the HTN&rsquo;s syntactic and structural consistency, rejecting undefined symbols and non-decomposable tasks, against established spatial and operational constraints. This verified logical sequence is subsequently compiled into a reactive Behavior Tree (BT) that guides execution through a fixed robotic skill library. During execution, a real-time object detection system and an atomic skill library dynamically translate the BT into grounded actions. Designed for human&ndash;robot collaborative environments, the architecture autonomously allocates standard operations to the robotic agent while safely deferring tasks requiring high dexterity to human operators. By combining the semantic adaptability of LLMs with the rigorous state validation of deterministic rule-based tools, this methodology is intended to reduce hallucination-driven failures and support safer manufacturing workflows, as evaluated through a system-level feasibility study rather than a component-wise ablation. The proposed architecture is evaluated against both physical and logical criteria using task-specific evaluation metrics. The framework was evaluated on four assembly tasks (T1&ndash;T4) using two Gemma model configurations, with 30 trials per task for each configuration (120 trials per configuration; 240 trials in total), achieving near-100% plan validity and near-zero hallucination rates under the higher-capacity configuration. Future integration of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies at the level of individual Behavior Tree leaves is discussed in Section Perception and Dynamic Adaptation as a promising direction to replace the current fixed robotic skill set.

title: Multi-Hazard Graph Artificial Intelligence for Infrastructure Resilience Screening in Romania: Integrating Ground Motion, Earth Observation, Hazard Exposure and Network Topology
abstract: Natural hazards can disrupt transport infrastructure through spatially heterogeneous flooding, seismic shaking, terrain conditions, and observed ground motion, while local exposure alone does not determine system-wide consequences. This study develops a reproducible multi-hazard Graph Artificial Intelligence framework for infrastructure resilience screening on the Romanian strategic road network. A frozen attributed line graph combines network topology with European land-cover, terrain, seismic, flood, and ground-motion evidence, and an independent disruption simulator provides continuous resilience-loss targets. GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT were trained under a leakage-controlled three-seed protocol. On the blind 194-scenario PRIMARY TEST, ensemble RMSE/R2 were 0.013343/0.997104 for GCN, 0.013978/0.996822 for GraphSAGE, and 0.015830/0.995924 for GAT. A fresh GCN branch achieved RMSE/R2 = 0.018230/0.995852 on 111 component-disjoint cases and 0.010468/0.991654 on 256 severity-specific held-out cases.
