Under 4-bit quantization, it retains an AUROC = 0.95 with a 4.02 GB memory footprint. These results show that a compact GPU-native implementation of activation-space monitoring can provide effective, retraining-free backdoor detection for real-time transformer inference.</jats:p>

title: Mixed-Precision Logarithmic Quantization for Efficient Neural Network Inference on FPGAs_supp1-3730233.mp4
DVFS for Small Language Model Inference on Mobile Edge Devices
TRIAD: Co-designing mixed-precision quantization, operator fusion, and on-chip memory reuse for real-time vision–language–action inference on automotive NPUs

Quantization Techniques for Efficient Inference of
Large Language Models
abstract:
<jats:p>Our research presents a comprehensive evaluation of quantization techniques applied to
transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs). We investigate Post-Training Quantization
(PTQ), Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), ultra-low-precision methods (INT4, INT3) and mixedprecision strategies. Practical experiments are conducted using toolchains such as Hugging Face
Transformers, AutoGPTQ and BitsAndBytes to quantize and deploy models like GPT-2, LLaMA 2
(7B) and Mistral (7B). Runtime performance, memory footprint and output quality are compared
across full-precision (FP16/FP32) and quantized (INT8/INT4) versions under consistent input and
inference settings. Our results show that quantization offers substantial performance gains, up to
40% faster inference.</jats:p>

title: Runtime Adaptive FPGA Architecture for Dynamic Language Model Inference in Intelligent Vehicles
abstract: <jats:p>Runtime adaptive FPGA execution is attractive for in-vehicle language models because the dominant bottleneck changes with context length, inference phase, and memory pressure. This work develops a ZCU102/XCZU9EG-oriented architecture with four constant-budget modes that redistribute 2,048 DSPs between attention and feed-forward processing under a stateful break-even controller. Evaluation combines checkpoint-level W8A8 screening, benchmark-derived automotive request statistics, analytical and event models, and Monte Carlo controller experiments. For SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, W8A8 screening increases WikiText-2 perplexity by 2.95%; 390,510 STRIDE-QA human turns have a median length of 14 tokens and p95 of 48. The compute model predicts an attention-heavy-mode benefit of 22.01% at 8,192 tokens. Across twenty independent 1,000-request traces per workload, the controller reduces mean modeled request latency by 1.68% for routine traffic, 16.75% for multimodal traffic, and 17.49% for long-context bursts relative to static C0. Executed W8A8 operator tests report 1.38–1.77% normalized RMSE and cosine similarity above 0.99984. These results support context-aware, transition-cost-aware resource allocation for adaptive edge language-model acceleration.</jats:p>

title: Capability, ranking dynamics, and inference pricing in the large language model ecosystem: evidence from linked public data
abstract: Public leaderboards and pricing catalogues offer complementary but hard-to-combine views of the large language model ecosystem. We analyse three linked public sources: an archived Open LLM Leaderboard v2 sample of 4,565 open-weight evaluation records with complete six-benchmark scores; an 89-snapshot human-preference panel of 279 models (June 2024–August 2025); and 2,685 priced chat endpoints (October 2026). Principal component analysis identifies a dominant common component (74% of benchmark variance), retained by parallel analysis and robust to family deduplication. Benchmark performance rises with parameter count (13.6 points per tenfold) and with submission date at constant size and type (10.5 points per year) under family-clustered inference. A documented change of the default rating on 20 May 2025 shifted all listed scores by about 18 points; within the stable period the preference frontier rose by about 187 points per year relative to a fixed reference set through 17 leaders with median spells of 12 days, top-20 slots concentrated among fewer organisations, and ratings did not drift within models. Among 201 models listed by three or more providers, the median maximum-to-minimum price ratio is 1.38 (1.27 under version-strict identifiers). A hedonic model adjusting for time since first listing attributes multipliers of about 3.1 to one standard deviation of arena score and 0.18 to open-weight status, robust to version-exact matching. Preference ratings and benchmark averages agree strongly for 69 matched models. Temporal mismatch, selective coverage, and related model families preclude causal interpretation.

title: Quantization-Induced Accuracy Degradation in Small Language Models: A Parametric Scaling Analysis
OBLIVION TextLM: A Query-relative Control Plane for Efficient Generative Language-model Inference
abstract: <jats:p>Long-context language models can ingest far more information than a particular query actually requires, yet retaining every represented distinction is neither equivalent to using it well nor automatically computationally efficient. We present OBLIVION TextLM, a model-agnostic query-relative control plane that operationalizes unresolved semantic obligations around a separately licensed pretrained language-model executor. The system constructs a live obligation state, routes evidence against that state, invokes the executor, permits new obligations to be born from intermediate evidence, generates evidence-bound completion certificates, verifies discharge conservatively, and retires an obligation only when verification and an explicit net-gain audit both succeed. Three matched modes—full-context baseline, retrieval-augmented generation, and OBLIVION—use the same executor to separate foundation-model quality from retrieval and control effects. The v2.0.0 reference implementation adds hybrid routing, citations, memory, streaming OpenAI-compatible clients, verifier separation, tracing, usage accounting, benchmarking, safety utilities, and advisory KV-cache ownership hooks. We validate the artifact by compilation, 29 automated tests, release-metadata checks, and deterministic three-mode smoke runs. We deliberately distinguish text-level semantic retirement from unmeasured physical KV-cache or GPU savings. The contribution is an executable, falsifiable systems framework for testing when verified query-relative state control improves quality–compute trade-offs without claiming a separately trained foundation model of its own.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Virtual Inertia: Dynamic Quantization of LLM Inference for Fast Frequency Response via Stochastic Impulse Control
abstract: <jats:p>As gigawatt-scale AI workloads strain low-inertia grids, traditional demand response fails to address stability crises due to critical timescale mismatches. This paper introduces Joule-per-Token Arbitrage, a stochastic control framework treating inference precision as a liquid control variable capable of sub-cycle actuation. We formulate the grid-compute nexus as a Stochastic Hybrid System (SHS), deriving an optimal control policy via Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Quasi-Variational Inequalities (HJB-QVI) to financialize Large Language Model (LLM) accuracy. Unlike binary load-shedding, our framework modulates GPU quantization states (FP16 → INT8 → INT4) to shed power with 16 ms latency while maintaining service continuity. Validated via a 2021 ERCOT Winter Storm Uri Digital Twin, simulations demonstrate a 1 GW AI cluster stabilizes frequency nadir 3× faster than conventional inertia (improving nadir from 59.30 Hz to 59.52 Hz). This prevents Tier-1 load shedding and reduces Rate-of-Change-of-Frequency (RoCoF) by 33%, with <5% transient perplexity increase. This work quantifies the thermodynamic exchange between computational intelligence and grid inertia, providing a pathway for gigawatt-scale virtual synchronous machines derived from algorithmic flexibility.</jats:p>

title: QAQ: Query-Adaptive Quantization for Large Language Model Inference
Hardware-Assisted Dynamic Quantization for Low-Power DNN Inference on Edge FPGAs
abstract: <jats:p>Energy efficiency poses a significant challenge when deploying Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) on resource-constrained Edge AI hardware. Traditional quantization strategies often rely on a fixed bit-width during execution, creating a rigid trade-off between energy consumption, latency, and network accuracy. To tackle this issue, we introduce a hardware-assisted dynamic quantization control framework leveraging a Hardware/Software Co-Design approach, capable of dynamic precision scaling across a wide spectrum from 16-bit down to 2-bit. By implementing a lightweight ingress FIFO buffer at the FPGA hardware level, the system observes input stream congestion in real time and autonomously orchestrates precision-control signals on the fly, mitigating simulated buffer backlog and suppressing frame drops during burst traffic scenarios. A hysteresis-damped hardware finite state machine (FSM) controller is integrated to ensure operational stability without host-CPU intervention. Experimental evaluation via PyTorch-based co-simulation alongside physical hardware synthesis on an AMD Xilinx Zynq-7000 FPGA (Digilent ZedBoard) using the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB) demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves 94.35% ± 0.05% Top-1 accuracy across five independent evaluation runs, matching the 16-bit baseline within 0.02 pp, while dynamically relieving queue pressure. Furthermore, the dedicated control-plane logic incurs a low resource footprint utilizing less than 0.01% of FPGA logic resources (three LUTs and one Flip-Flop) and a standalone dynamic power of 7.0 mW (projected to <1.0 mW for core logic in integrated SoCs), providing an autonomous, low-overhead supervisory control mechanism for adaptive edge inference.</jats:p>

title: Adapting a small language model for plant protection information in Türkiye
abstract: Plant protection advice must connect biological knowledge with product use, legal conditions, and evidence from sources. A fluent answer can omit a restriction or confuse a residue limit with permission to use a product. Small language models offer a practical route to local information services. However, local model training does not show that agricultural advice is reliable. This study examines BitkiKorumacı, a Turkish system that combines a source database with adaptation of a small language model. Four development configurations use a four-bit Qwen3 model with four billion parameters and low-rank adaptation. The analysis compares archived answers with and without added database evidence. It covers 860 cases across 14 task categories. Developers repeatedly used this evaluation set, so the results describe development performance. The B2S configuration passed the automatic answer criterion on 112 of 860 cases without added retrieval and 601 cases with retrieval. These results correspond to 13.02% and 69.88%. B2S with added retrieval met 12 of 14 category thresholds. It still failed the resistance task, the source-based examination task, and separate behavior checks. All four configurations still had behavior failures. All 1,000 benchmark cases lack completed independent expert review. The campaign revised 285 references as passage-based assistant drafts. In passage tasks, added retrieval did not improve the pooled score. Most of the overall increase occurred in categories that received extra database context. The results show that local adaptation can improve the use of supplied evidence within this task design. They do not show field accuracy or the safety of autonomous advice. The study gives a documented development case for Turkish plant protection and lists the tests necessary before practical use.

title: Towards Efficient Vision-Language Model Inference via Stepwise Visual Token Pruning
abstract: <jats:p>Vision-Language Models (VLMs) generate hundreds to thousands of visual tokens per image, making token-dependent computation across decoder layers, including projection, FFN, and attention, as well as KV-cache memory, a major inference bottleneck. Existing token pruning methods address this issue in two ways. Pre-decoder pruning shortens the input sequence but cannot account for the textual query, whereas in-decoder pruning enables query-aware selection but retains the full token cost in early decoder layers. We show that these two strategies are structurally complementary and propose a training-free two-stage framework that exploits this complementarity through stepwise token reduction. In the first stage, CaNS (CLS-Attention Neighbor Selection) performs spatially coherent pre-decoder pruning to shorten the sequence while preserving salient regions. In the second stage, DaFT (Dual-Attention Filtered Token Pruning) refines visual tokens within the decoder usinga V2T→T2V dual-attention mechanism for query-conditioned selection. On LLaVA-1.5, our method reduces 576 visual tokens to 32, a 94.4% reduction, while retaining 97.1% of the baseline performance and reducing FLOPs to 27.9% of the baseline decoder cost, or 37.8% of the full-model cost including the vision encoder. It also generalizes to LLaVA-NeXT, achieving up to a 3.00× speedup under aggressive compression.</jats:p>

title: Reusing obsolete windows 10 PCs for on-premises large language model inference
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The Windows 10 end-of-life provides a material incentive to repurpose legacy PCs as on-premises large language model (LLM) inference servers. This study assesses the technical feasibility, economic viability and the environmental and social issues of converting an enterprise workstation with an NVIDIA Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) into a dedicated AI node. Using Proxmox virtualisation, Ollama, and Open WebUI to benchmark several open-source LLMs, this study shows that a repurposed workstation, fitted with a single consumer-grade NVIDIA GPU, can deliver stable inference throughput of 29–65 tokens/s for bounded, conversational coding and document-assistant workflows, while preserving full data sovereignty and eliminating recurring subscription fees. Performance analysis reveals that resource contention and GPU memory allocation are the primary determinants of throughput. Correctness, assessed against three established public benchmarks with gold answers, does not track the same ranking as throughput; combining both axes identifies gemma4:e4b as the strongest model evaluated on this hardware for both speed and correctness, while the slowest model tested was among the most accurate. A cost-benefit model shows local operation is substantially cheaper than mid-range and premium cloud alternatives, and only modestly costlier than the cheapest cloud tier on a per-prompt basis—a gap this study argues is outweighed by the digital-sovereignty benefits of local control, particularly where compliance-driven data-handling constraints apply. The study summarizes key background motivations for on-premises AI—privacy, security, regulatory risk—and estimates that this repurposed workstation's usage-phase
                    <jats:italic>CO</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    e footprint is lower than each of the cloud alternatives compared, in addition to avoiding the embodied manufacturing emissions of new hardware. Repurposing legacy workstations with readily available open source tools offers a sustainable, cost-effective pathway for organizations to deploy practical LLM inference capabilities locally, providing a strategic alternative to cloud services for entities that prioritize privacy, regulatory compliance or long-term cost containment.
                  </jats:p>

title: Post-Training Low-Bit Quantization for Edge-Sensor Neural Inference
TMXVAR: Twin Microscaling Floating-Point Quantization for Efficient Visual Autoregressive Model Inference on FPGA
Neuro-Fetcher: An Asynchronous Learning-Based Key-Value Cache Pre-fetching Pipeline for Efficient Large Language Model Inference
abstract: <jats:p>The immense size of the Key-Value (KV) cache in Large Language Models (LLMs) has made autoregressive inference a significant memory-bandwidth bottleneck. Recent KV cache compression methods mainly utilize handcraft or heuristic rules to pre-fetch the important KV cache entries and emit unnecessary caches. These rule-based methods fail to capture the complex dynamic attention patterns inherent in different models and data distributions, leading to degradation of downstream tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel learning-based KV cache management approach named Neuro-Fetcher, which is a lightweight neural network trained to accurately predict important KV cache entries by the relationship between input tokens and intermediate attention patterns. This learning-based pre-fetching strategy can improve the accuracy of KV cache prediction and the performance of downstream tasks. Our work overcomes two critical challenges for learning-based pre-fetchers: we propose the "Shallow Pre-fetching" strategy to tackle the high complexity of multi-layer prediction, and design a "Ping-Pong Scheduling" mechanism to effectively hide the inference latency of the predictor itself. The experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves inference throughput over strong heuristic baselines without compromising model perplexity. Furthermore, we conduct an analysis of the model generalization capabilities and demonstrate that our Neuro-Fetcher could exhibit strong zero-shot intra-family transferability (e.g., OPT-13B to OPT-6.7B), unlocking a &apos;train-once, deploy-anywhere within the family&apos; paradigm that drastically reduces deployment costs.</jats:p>

title: Fully Quantized Training vs. Post-Training Quantization for a Small Hyperspectral Transformer Model for Pixel-Level Foreign Plastic Object Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Low-precision floating-point computation has become central to efficient artificial intelligence, yet its behavior for compact transformer-based hyperspectral imaging (HSI) models remains underexplored. In this work, we present a controlled comparative study of fully quantized training (FQT) and post-training quantization (PTQ) for pixel-wise foreign plastic object (FPO) classification in poultry hyperspectral data. Using a fixed state-of-the-art spatial–spectral transformer backbone, a common mixed-precision strategy, and identical training and inference protocols, we evaluate FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 across predictive performance, model compression, training efficiency, and inference efficiency. The results show that mixed-precision FQT remains highly robust across the tested precision spectrum, with all reduced-precision configurations staying within 0.63 percentage points of the FP32 baseline in overall accuracy while consistently outperforming PTQ at matched precisions. Across the evaluated formats, BF16 provides the closest accuracy to FP32, whereas FP8 offers a particularly favorable balance between accuracy preservation and reduced precision, while model compression increases progressively to 3.69× under NVFP4. The computational benefits, however, are strongly workload dependent. Native FP8/FP4 hardware support does not automatically improve training throughput for this compact model at moderate workloads, and the larger training batches required to better utilize low-precision hardware can degrade predictive performance. In contrast, large-batch inference can effectively exploit FP8 and NVFP4 without affecting predictive accuracy. An ablation study further shows that selective retention of numerically sensitive modules in FP32 is essential for stable ultra-low-precision operation. Overall, the findings demonstrate that low precision is a viable but workload-dependent design choice for compact HSI transformers, with FQT providing greater accuracy robustness than PTQ and FP8, offering a favorable overall accuracy–efficiency trade-off.</jats:p>

title: Characterizing KV-Cache Performance in Large Language Model Inference: Context Length, Attention Architecture, and GPU Memory Residency
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) commonly employ key–value (KV) caching to avoid recomputing previous attention states during autoregressive inference. However, its measured performance benefit depends on workload characteristics and the memory environment. This study presents a controlled systems characterization of KV-cache performance across input context length, grouped-query attention configurations, and GPU-memory residency. Experiments use Qwen2.5-3B and SmolLM3-3B under verified fully resident conditions with fixed 128-token generation, prompt lengths from 128 to 2048 tokens, randomized cache-enabled/cache-disabled execution, GPU telemetry, and repeated paired validation. KV-cache speedup increases from 1.34× to 8.31× for Qwen2.5-3B and from 1.28× to 8.62× for SmolLM3-3B. At 2048 prompt tokens, 30 randomized paired trials confirm mean speedups of 8.10× and 8.51×, corresponding to runtime reductions of 87.65% and 88.25%, while physical GPU-memory utilization remains below 61%. Despite SmolLM3-3B requiring twice the theoretical KV-cache storage per token, both models show comparable context-dependent scaling in the fully resident regime. A separate Mistral-7B case study further demonstrates that memory pressure can substantially alter apparent speedup. These results establish KV-cache speedup as workload- and system-dependent and demonstrate that meaningful benchmarking requires reporting context length, cache configuration, model and cache footprints, physical accelerator-memory residency, runtime, throughput, and relevant GPU-memory conditions during each inference experiment.</jats:p>

title: Dynamic Semantic Adaptation for Efficient Large Language Model Inference
A Survey on Quantization Techniques for Large Language Models
abstract: <jats:p>Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across modern language tasks, but their significant computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on limited hardware. To overcome this, quantization—reducing numerical precision from 32-bit to lower-bit formats such as 4-bit—has emerged as an effective compression method to minimize model size and enhance inference efficiency. The objective of this paper is to review recent advancements in LLM quantization, outline the key challenges involved, and examine how different techniques attempt to address them. This review is based on a focused analysis of recent peer-reviewed studies and introduces a high-level taxonomy of modern methods, complemented by a comparative performance summary to illustrate their practical impact. Comparative analysis across selected papers highlights that quantization effectively reduces model size and memory consumption while maintaining near-original accuracy and significant inference speedups. In conclusion, modern quantization techniques strike an optimal balance between accuracy, efficiency, and resource utilization, enabling scalable and affordable deployment of large-scale AI models across diverse computing platforms.</jats:p>

title: Efficient Reasoning at the Edge: A Systematic Review of Small Reasoning Models, Test-Time Scaling, Quantization, and Energy-Aware AI Inference
Canonical and Compact Representations in Small Language Model Graph Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Small language models can classify graphs serialized as text, but three properties of graphs complicate the conversion: a graph has no intrinsic vertex order, so one graph yields many texts; explicit serializations are long under a fixed input budget; and one serialization shows only a single view of the structure. We evaluate the corresponding design responses under one protocol. Raw adjacency and edge lists are compared with a degree-sorted ordering, two exact canonical serializations, a deterministic BFS profile, compact Graph6 and NetLSD encodings, soft-prompt baselines, and validation-weighted late fusion. On five TUDataset benchmarks and three instruction-tuned small language models, the exact canonical serializations improve over raw adjacency lists in 14 of the 15 settings, and late fusion improves on that baseline in all 15. The compact encodings shorten the input by 67.7% and 42.2%, respectively, and both exceed the baseline in mean accuracy. A paired analysis with correction for multiple comparisons confirms the gain for both canonical serializations, the deterministic profile, the degree-sorted ordering, NetLSD, and late fusion. Serialization is therefore a consequential modeling decision, not merely a preprocessing step. This study provides an empirical basis for that decision by measuring accuracy, permutation robustness, input length, and preprocessing cost under a single protocol.</jats:p>

title: REFINE-Verilog: Reliability-Based Fine-Tuning and Inference Enhancement for Small Language Model in Partial Verilog Generation
Enabling Efficient Serverless Inference Serving for LLM (Large Language Model) in the Cloud
abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en">This review report examines the problem of cold-start latency in serverless inference for large language models (LLMs) and surveys recent systems that address it, with a particular focus on ServerlessLLM. In serverless environments, loading multi-hundred-gigabyte LLM checkpoints and initializing GPU resources can dominate end-to-end latency, making real-time applications such as conversational agents and translation services difficult to deploy cost-efficiently. The report first summarizes the cold-start problem and common mitigation strategies in today's Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) platforms, including container warming, host-side checkpoint caching, and cluster-level storage servers. It then reviews the design of ServerlessLLM, which exploits underutilized multi-tier storage in GPU servers, a loading-optimized checkpoint format, live inference migration based on token-level state transfer, and a startup-time-aware model scheduler. Additional methods from recent literature, such as RainbowCake's layered container caching, and the cold-start handling mechanisms of major cloud providers are also discussed. Drawing on the evaluation presented in the original work, the report highlights that multi-tier checkpoint loading and live migration reduce model startup time by up to 6-8× compared to conventional formats, and deliver up to 28× lower startup latency than Ray Serve for large models in realistic traces. The review concludes by outlining open challenges and future directions, including integrating model compression, multi-level inference pipelines, and advanced memory-offloading techniques to further improve the scalability and efficiency of serverless LLM inference.</jats:p>

title: SGLite: A Compact Serving Framework for Large Language Model Inference
Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models: A Review and Exploratory Small-Model Pilot
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent responses that are false, unsupported, outdated, or more certain than the available evidence justifies. This manuscript presents a narrative review of major hallucination-mitigation approaches and an exploratory pilot intended to refine a future evaluation protocol rather than establish model-level performance. The review covers false-premise handling, abstention and knowledge-boundary estimation, retrieval-augmented generation, grounding, verification, self-checking, and multimodal hallucination. It also distinguishes published evidence from an engineering proposal for failure-driven correction. The pilot used a locally executed interface labeled Gemma 3 1B-IT and ten hand-designed stress prompts spanning false premises, insufficient evidence, fabricated-citation traps, unknowable events, and future-value requests. The revised analysis deliberately avoids compressing these observations into a single hallucination score. Two responses were epistemically appropriate, three were partially appropriate but introduced unsupported content, and five failed the target behavior. Generation stability was tracked separately: one otherwise appropriate answer entered a repetition loop, and another item required a restart after a context-length error. An extended follow-up run was terminated when the local system became unstable and began returning empty outputs; those observations are reported only qualitatively. The pilot is too small and insufficiently controlled to support causal claims or generalization to the Gemma family. Its value is methodological: it illustrates why hallucination research should report multiple axes - factual correctness, false-premise resistance, correct abstention, unnecessary abstention, grounding fidelity, coverage, calibration where available, and generation stability - rather than one aggregate number. The literature further suggests that mitigation is most credible when model behavior, external evidence, verification, and evaluation design are treated as a coupled system.</jats:p>

title: Comparative Evaluation of GGUF and GPTQ Quantization for Llama 3.1 Inference on x86 and ARM Architectures
Adaptive Quantization Strategies for Robust ML Inference Under Distribution Shift
LIQOS-ViT: Learned Importance guided Quantization with Outlier awareness for Split inference ViTs
MindCore: A Safety-Gated, Memory-Augmented Small Language Model Architecture for Culturally Adapted Mental Wellness Support in India
abstract: <jats:p>Mental health support in India faces a large treatment gap, and small language models (SLMs) are attractive for low-cost wellness applications but raise open questions about safety, memory and clinical validity. We describe MindCore, a wellness-support system built around a LoRA-adapted Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct model, and a control architecture that wraps the model with three components: (i) a deterministic multilingual crisis gate that bypasses the model and returns helpline information; (ii) a conversational administration of the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 questionnaires, framed strictly as self-assessment and not diagnosis; and (iii) a three-layer memory (working, episodic, semantic) with exact timestamps that lets the system recall earlier sessions after days or months. We evaluate the components that do not require GPU inference on author-constructed test sets (36 crisis and 33 non-crisis messages in English, Hinglish and Hindi; 26 focus-classification items; 39 questionnaire answers; 20 synthetic users). The first version only labelled crisis language without acting on it and flagged 7 of 26 explicit crisis statements (26.9%). The gated version flagged 23 of 26 (88.5%) and, after a patch made in response to the observed failures, 26 of 26 on the same development set, but flagged none of 10 indirect expressions of hopelessness (95% CI 0-28%). Testing also exposed defects such as scoring "I don't know" as "not at all". Keyword memory retrieval reached 80% Hit@3 for lexically matching queries but 50% for paraphrases, close to a 40% recency-only baseline. The language model was not evaluated end to end, no human participants were involved, and no clinical validity is claimed. We discuss limitations, regulatory and privacy considerations, and a roadmap toward clinician-reviewed evaluation.</jats:p>

title: Mixed-Precision Logarithmic Quantization for Efficient Neural Network Inference on FPGAs
Inference in Motion: Memory-Centric Co-Design for Large Language Models
How Elicitation Shapes Model Preferences: A Study of Small Language Models
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models are increasingly used to elicit value judgments and preference data, but this immediately raises a simple question: when we ask a model what it prefers, are we actually measuring a stable preference, or are we partly measuring the way we asked the question? We conduct a controlled empirical study of preference elicitation in three small instruction-tuned language models: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Gemma-2-2B-it, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. We construct 20 value-laden outcomes spanning five semantic categories and evaluate every one of the 190 unique outcome pairs using three pairwise elicitation protocols-forced choice, reasoningassisted choice, and probability elicitation-together with an independent scalar-rating protocol. We measure response validity, Option-A selection tendency, cross-method agreement, cross-model agreement, category-level Bradley-Terry preference structure, and consistency between scalar ratings and pairwise choices. The results reveal substantial elicitation-dependent variation in observed preferences. For example, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct selects Option A in 51.6% of forced-choice comparisons but 96.8% of reasoning-assisted comparisons, while Gemma-2-2B-it selects Option A in 93.2% of forced-choice comparisons but assigns a mean probability of only 16.1% to Option A under probability elicitation. Cross-method Cohen's kappa is generally low, with values as low as 0.024 for Qwen forced-choice versus reasoningassisted choice, 0.022 for Gemma forced-choice versus probability elicitation, and-0.017 for Llama reasoning-assisted choice versus probability elicitation. Together, these findings point to a simple but important conclusion: elicited preference should be interpreted as a measurement outcome conditional on the elicitation protocol, rather than automatically treated as a protocol-invariant readout of a latent model preference.</jats:p>

AdaMIQ: Adaptive Mutual Information Quantization for Vision-Language Models
abstract: <jats:p>Low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ) is essential for deploying vision-language models, but existing PTQ pipelines often allocate precision using uniform or local sensitivity rules that ignore cross-channel dependency. We propose AdaMIQ, an adaptive mutual-information quantization framework for compressing the language backbones of vision-language models without retraining. AdaMIQ estimates channel dependency from calibration activations, forms dependency-aware groups, assigns group-wise mixed precision with Hessian-guided importance, and compensates reconstruction error within each group; spectral clustering is used as a practical grouping refinement inside this pipeline rather than as the main source of gain. We evaluate AdaMIQ on the language backbones of LLaVA-1.6, Qwen3-VL-8B, and SmolVLM2-2.2B using perplexity benchmarks, downstream zero-shot tasks, cross-architecture transfer, ablations, calibration robustness, and time-memory analysis. The results show that AdaMIQ is strongest on LLaVA-1.6 and SmolVLM2-2.2B in the main 4-bit regime, with MI-guided grouping providing the largest component contribution and with no additional inference-time mechanism beyond the quantized weights. The method is therefore a practical dependency-aware PTQ strategy when an offline calibration pass is acceptable, while its mixed behavior on Qwen and its calibration sensitivity define clear boundaries for architecture-robust low-bit VLM compression.</jats:p>

Extraction of clinical information from faxed medical records using a small local large language model pipeline on consumer hardware
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Specialty referral packets often arrive by fax and clinicians must manually read and organize a large amount of disparate information to affect continuity of care. Commercial large language models (LLMs) can organize packet information, but protected health information (PHI) must be secured. We evaluated whether an open-weight pipeline running entirely on one consumer graphics card can accurately extract clinical information from faxed referral packets.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We generated 200 synthetic colorectal cancer referral packets from simulated patient records, rendered them as faxes without a text layer. A local pipeline transcribed each packet with an optical character recognition model (OvisOCR2) and extracted structured data with an open-weight LLM (Qwen3.8-27B). Twenty outcomes spanning patient identifiers, laboratory results, dates, diagnoses, procedures, medications, imaging, and event chronology were scored against ground truth on 140 validation packets.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Laboratory values were extracted exactly in 98.9% of 7879 instances, dates in 99.7%, diagnoses in 100%, and procedures in 92.9%. Timeline recall was 96.7% and precision 99.4%. Weighted accuracy was 0.990 (95% CI 0.987–0.992). None of 11,993 extracted facts were fabricated. Median processing time was 90 seconds per packet.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>An open-weight pipeline on consumer hardware accurately extracted multi-domain clinical information from synthetic faxed referrals.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>

title: Stage-Aware Optimization of Llama 3 Model Inference for Language Services on Many-Core CPUs
abstract: <jats:p>LLM-based language services (e.g., summarization, translation, and question answering) require low-latency and cost-effective inference, yet GPU resources may be costly, unavailable, or difficult to integrate in many deployments. Many-core CPUs provide a flexible alternative, but achieving efficient inference requires optimizations that match the distinct computational characteristics of the Prefill and Decode stages. This paper presents a stage-aware optimization approach for Llama 3 inference on two Phytium many-core processors (FT-2000+/64 and FT-1500A). Fine-grained profiling shows that matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) in the Decode stage accounts for 99.4% of Decode time, whereas Prefill exposes additional token-level parallelism. Accordingly, in Prefill we reorganize multiple token-wise MVM operations into matrix–matrix multiplication and select the GEMM implementation by micro-batch granularity, including a blocked C GEMM (up to 7.8× over token-wise MVM) and a LibShalom-based tile path. In Decode, we apply OpenMP-based intra-kernel parallelism to MVM, RMSNorm, Softmax, and attention-head computation. Experiments on representative GLUE workloads show that the self-kernel implementation improves time per output token (TPOT) by 1.67× at two threads (2.80× at eight). A complete baseline study then shows that a tuned BLAS GEMV accelerates the dominant Decode MVM by a further 3.1×; following the stage-aware selection principle, the final configuration reaches a TPOT of 141.9 ms—a 17.2× end-to-end speedup (7.05 tokens/s per 16-core node)—with scaling that continues to all cores. A kernel-level scalability study on Phytium FT-2000+/64 (Decode MVM up to 8.4× at eight threads) further shows that saturation beyond eight threads is a property of the kernel implementation rather than of the platform. These results demonstrate that stage-aware characterization and per-stage implementation selection can substantially improve single-request Llama 3 inference efficiency on many-core CPUs, and provide guidance for CPU-side optimization in language-service deployments.</jats:p>

title: MESO: Memory-Efficient Speculative Offloading for Large Language Model Inference
Prompt-Shape- and Prefix-Cache-Aware CPU/NPU Routing for Large Language Model Inference on Edge SoCs
abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) inference on edge systems must exploit heterogeneous central processing unit (CPU) and neural processing unit (NPU) resources under tight memory and latency constraints. Because prefilling and autoregressive decoding have different computational characteristics, the fastest backend depends on the request shape and prefix-cache reuse. This work proposes request-level CPU/NPU routing for the RK3588 system on chip (SoC). Prompt-shape-aware routing (PSR) uses prompt length and generation budget to select a backend for no-cache requests, while prefix-cache-aware routing (PCAR) additionally models reusable-prefix length, remaining prefill workload, full-context effects, and cache-path state with backend-specific latency models. On 49 no-cache held-out workloads, PSR achieves 97.96% backend-selection accuracy and a relative oracle loss of 0.121% ± 0.010%. On 45 independent cache-aware held-out workloads, accounting for the remaining prefill workload reduces relative oracle loss from 4.926% ± 0.378% for PSR(raw) to 0.425% ± 0.060% for PSR(eff). The complete PCAR model further reduces it to 0.205% ± 0.043%, improves selection accuracy from 93.33% to 95.56%, and provides an additional 0.22% cumulative-latency reduction over that of PSR(eff). These results show that jointly modeling request shape and prefix-cache state enables near-oracle heterogeneous LLM inference routing on edge SoCs.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Disclosure: Reframing Privacy as Inference Impedance in Large Language Models
abstract:
<jats:p>Contemporary debates in AI ethics continue to frame privacy primarily in terms of disclosure, identifiability, and data access.
This article argues that such a framing is no longer sufficient for embedding-based artificial intelligence systems. We introduce
the Deep Personal Privacy (DPP) framework, which reconceptualizes privacy as inference impedance within high-dimensional
semantic representation spaces. Rather than asking whether information has been revealed, DPP evaluates how easily sensitive
attributes can be inferred from latent embeddings. We model embedding spaces as semantic transmission layers that enable
indirect attribute inference through geometric alignment. Privacy risk is therefore defined in terms of cosine similarity, inference
probability, and logarithmic impedance within structured inference graphs. The framework integrates ontology-driven
sensitive expression mapping, representation-level perturbation mechanisms, and a multi-objective optimization procedure
balancing utility and privacy. mpirical demonstrations show that DPP-based interventions reduce semantic alignment with
sensitive concept prototypes and increase inference resistance while maintaining acceptable task erformance. Conceptually,
the framework advances a paradigm shift in AI ethics: privacy must be evaluated not only by what systems disclose, but by what
they are capable of inferring. DPP thus complements existing structural and statistical privacy approaches by introducing a
representation-level metric for inferential power asymmetry</jats:p>

Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models: A Survey
abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory and compute costs of large language model (LLM) inference by converting a pretrained model from floating-point weights and activations to lower-precision representations after training. Recent studies have shown that LLMs can be compressed to low-bit representations (eg. 4-bit and 2-bit) with minimal performance degradation. As a result, PTQ has become a standard tool for the efficient deployment of large language models. However, the rapid development of quantization methods has created a fragmented landscape, where approaches differ in error mitigation strategies, calibration procedures, and hardware assumptions, making systematic comparison difficult.
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 This survey organizes PTQ for LLMs around a single question: How does each method control quantization error? We group existing approaches into four families: compensation-based methods correct errors after quantization, often using Hessian information or low-rank residual terms; rotation-based methods apply orthogonal transforms to redistribute outliers before quantization; salience-based methods identify and protect the weights or channels that matter most; and optimization-based methods learn rounding, clipping, or scaling parameters directly from calibration data.
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 Beyond this taxonomy, we analyze how individual transformer components, such as attention projections and normalization layers, respond differently to precision loss. We also review calibration strategies, from simple min-max ranges to activation-aware and reconstruction-based approaches, and discuss how the choice of calibration data affects robustness. Finally, we outline open challenges: extreme low-bit quantization, native hardware formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4, quantizing new architectures like mixture-of-experts and state-space models, and the effect of quantization on long-context and reasoning workloads.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 By unifying taxonomy, component-level analysis, and calibration strategy in one framework, this survey aims to give researchers and practitioners a clear, practical reference for understanding and deploying quantized LLMs. We also provide a repository to track developments in this evolving field: https://github.com/FDataLab/LLMQuantizationSurvey.&nbsp;
</div></jats:p>

Efficient Adaptation of Large Language Models: A Survey of Parameter-Efficient, Quantization-Aware, and Alignment-Stage Tuning
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) pre-trained on web-scale data are now the default substrate for natural-language systems, and the same recipe increasingly powers multimodal models. As these models reach tens to hundreds of billions of parameters, the central practical question has shifted from how to train them to how to adapt them efficiently: full fine-tuning is memory-bound, storage-bound, and energy-intensive. This survey provides an up-to-date, systematically organized map of efficient adaptation of LLMs across three complementary layers. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) updates only a small fraction of weights through adapters, low-rank reparameterizations (LoRA, AdaLoRA, DoRA, VeRA), prompt-based, and selective methods. Quantization-aware and memory-efficient adaptation (QLoRA, LoftQ, QA-LoRA) couples low-bit backbones with trainable adapters so that billion-parameter models can be tuned on a single GPU. Alignment-stage tuning, via supervised instruction tuning and preference optimization (RLHF, DPO and its variants KTO, ORPO, SimPO, IPO), shapes behavior rather than task accuracy alone. We extend the scope to multimodal adaptation and to emerging modular and mixture-of-experts adapters. Beyond a taxonomy, our two central contributions are the Adaptation Cube, a unifying framework that positions methods along parameter, memory, and alignment efficiency, and a controlled comparison of six representative methods (LoRA, PiSSA, DoRA, QLoRA, VeRA, (IA)³) on a common backbone and harness. We further provide a documented search and selection strategy, an efficiency accounting that includes energy and carbon, and a hardware-oriented deployment guide. The survey is intended as a current reference for researchers and practitioners selecting an adaptation strategy under real resource constraints.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Protected least-sufficient reconstruction (PLSR) is applied to a codimension-three timelike Codazzi defect with a primitive projective link and two non-scalar source grades. Exact marked recovery selects E3 ⊕ E2 and M3(C) ⊕ M2(C). Primitive multiplication unifies the projective exact sequence, the rigid (2, 3) correspondence, its Green metric, the minimal rank-five Hermitian carrier, and a structural dark port line. Centered determinant/Clifford completion gives S(U(3) × U(2)), the primitive Z6 quotient, chiral 16-plets, and kY = 5/3; the integral A2 branch gives the three-state family orbit and primitive commensurate norm-seven class. One Alena-Codazzi response supplies typed realization tests. Its finite realization combines the upstream source/local incidences with three executable packets: a marked four-moment primitive-port certificate, a control-basis-invariant scalar/trace susceptibility residual, and a common-root holonomy test whose remaining primitive-root lift is one Z2 bit. After the stated exact reduced attachments, the scale-free response is a one-dimensional saturation manifold with global coordinate u and a discrete norm-seven orientation. One predeclared scale-free observable may locate u; the remaining continuous CKM, PMNS, neutral-shape, and bosonic coordinates are no-retune tests. Absolute normalization, continuum poles and lifetimes, and precision matching remain separate completion problems.</jats:p>

miRstring: An RNA language model enables mature miRNA decoding and artificial small RNA design across species
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are processed from structured precursors and subsequently loaded into Argonaute proteins to repress target mRNAs. Accurate decoding of mature miRNAs from precursor sequences is fundamental to miRNA annotation and the rational engineering of artificial miRNAs. However, existing computational approaches are largely developed for humans, with limited ability to generalize across diverse plants, animals, and viruses. Moreover, a unified data-driven framework that links mature-miRNA decoding with the predictive design of artificial miRNA precursors is still lacking, restricting the scalable application of miRNA biotechnology across species.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We develop and evaluate miRstring, a biogenesis-aware RNA language framework for decoding the four boundaries of mature miRNAs from precursor context across species, and further investigate its utility for cross-species miRNA annotation and rational artificial miRNA design.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>miRstring, a biogenesis-aware RNA language framework, was developed using 77,708 miRNA precursors spanning 414 species. The model was evaluated against existing methods under both family-held-out and species-held-out settings to assess its ability to generalize to unseen miRNA families and species. Attention-based analyses were further performed to examine whether miRstring captured biologically relevant features associated with miRNA processing, and the framework was subsequently applied to predictive design of artificial miRNA precursors.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>miRstring substantially outperformed existing methods across species-held-out evaluations and, notably, retained strong performance under the more stringent family-held-out setting. It accurately identified mature-miRNA start sites, while attention was enriched at endonuclease-cleaved miRNA/miRNA* boundaries, revealing biologically meaningful processing features. Importantly, miRstring-guided precursor design markedly enhanced artificial miRNA-mediated target repression, demonstrating its utility for rational miRNA engineering.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>miRstring provides a scalable framework linking cross-species mature-miRNA annotation with predictive artificial miRNA design, extending computational miRNA analysis toward artificial intelligence-driven small-RNA biotechnology.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>

title: Protected Reconstruction from Codazzi Defects: Equianharmonic Quantization and a Minimal Standard-Model Carrier
abstract: <jats:p>A geometric reconstruction framework is developed in which protected data of a codimension-three timelike Codazzi defect determine both a finite internal structure and a constrained low-energy prediction manifold. Protected least-sufficient reconstruction selects a primitive $3+2$ carrier, its multiplication and dark-line geometry, the global form $S(U(3)\times U(2))$, a chiral $16$-dimensional coefficient packet with $k_Y=5/3$, and a norm-seven family structure. These data are embedded in a single Alena-Codazzi Parent action. Its conserved charge provides an intrinsic selector $\chi_Q=dQ/d\Omega$; directional bounds, Fredholm-Feshbach reduction, and validated continuation give sufficient conditions for a unique first protected constrained fold without assuming global charge convexity. The selected Parent state fixes a single scale-free coordinate $u_*$ and simultaneously determines a rank-one critical-response residue that can be recovered from stable-side data with certified second-order error. This gives independent tests of the critical direction, its transport into family and dark sectors, and proposed causal relations between them. The resulting charged-family shapes form fixed-Casimir $A_2$ circles, while norm-seven and contraction-Wilson data organize hierarchy and CP orientation. Spectral states and dark-channel widths are treated separately through Schur-Herglotz, Hankel, and outgoing-channel tests. After one global calibration, electroweak, charged-family, CKM, and Dirac-PMNS observables are constrained to a one-dimensional no-retune manifold. Absolute normalization, Majorana data, and continuum scattering remain independent completion problems.</jats:p>

Weak Distributive Inference in Language Acquisition
abstract: We find that children compute distributive inferences, and thus that they are capable pragmatic reasoners when alternatives can be derived without lexical substitution. This provides further evidence that they are not limited by other factors like working memory or pragmatic tolerance. In addition, we find evidence that children consistently computed weak distributive inferences. In the spirit of Fox’s (2007) grammatical account, such inferences require double application of Exh, one scoping above the universal quantifier and another below. Thus, not only do children compute implicatures, but they appear to adopt the more complex parse—embedding one operator inside another—rather than relying on the simpler, global option that generates a strong distributive inference.

Does Lower Precision Always Save Energy? Benchmarking Energy–Performance Trade-Offs in Weight-Quantized Large Language Model Inference on a GPU
abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) inference is an increasing component of AI energy demand, while the energy effects of weight quantization depend on workload phase and implementation. We benchmarked four LLM families—Gemma 4 E4B IT, Qwen3.5 4B, Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, and Ministral 3 3B Instruct—across Q4_K_M, Q6_K, Q8_0, and BF16 weight representations on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 using llama.cpp/CUDA. Five workloads separated prefill from autoregressive generation, and GPU energy was estimated from NVML telemetry. In PP-512, no statistically significant differences were detected under the employed measurement protocol; in PP-1024, precision affected total energy and mean GPU power. In all generation scenarios, model family, precision, and their interaction significantly affected the primary endpoints. Relative to BF16, Q4_K_M reduced dynamic energy per token by 63.6–85.7% and increased generation throughput by 85.2–160.2% across all four model families. Ministral 3 3B Instruct–Q4_K_M ranked first in TOPSIS, whereas Nemotron 3 Nano 4B–Q4_K_M required less GPU memory. Findings are limited to single-request execution on one RTX 4090/llama.cpp-CUDA stack; output quality was not assessed, and 50 ms NVML sampling limits interpretation of short prefill measurements.</jats:p>

title: Fall-Related Safety Hazard Analysis in Construction Using Vision-Language Models and Natural Language Inference
abstract: <jats:p>Fall accidents account for more than one-third of fatalities in construction, and fall-related hazards introduce a significant risk of occupational injuries to construction workers. Although numerous efforts have been devoted to preventing falls, most studies have focused on detecting predefined hazards, with less consideration of understanding the context in which hazardous conditions arise. Most previous studies are limited in identifying combined hazardous conditions, consisting of multiple safety violations, such as a missing safety lanyard on an unprotected open edge on a scaffold. In this context, this study proposes an integrated fall hazard analysis framework using a vision-language model that converts visual information into hazard-descriptions aligned with legal safety standards. Then, the framework analyzes the hazard-related texts using natural language inference to recognize the risk of hazards. By leveraging the BLIP-2 architecture, the proposed method establishes independent image captioning models for three critical categories directly associated with fall accidents: openings, scaffolding, and worker behavior. The framework classifies images as “Safe” or “Risk” based on generated descriptions that strictly adhere to occupational safety and health standards. The proposed fall-hazard assessment framework achieves an F1-score of 0.84, indicating its significant practical potential for comprehensive fall hazard analysis in real-world construction environments.</jats:p>

title: Inference Without Stakes: What Large Language Models Do-and Do Not-Show About Intelligence
abstract: <jats:p>Large language models have made a powerful case for the reach of statistical inference. They produce fluent language, solve heterogeneous problems, and exhibit forms of abstraction that cannot be dismissed as simple retrieval. Their success, however, does not establish that inference is sufficient for intelligence. That conclusion follows only by sliding between distinct ideas: inferential competence, task performance, agency, and phenomenal awareness. This essay separates them. It argues that inference is always organized by a prior structure of relevance-a specification of which distinctions, errors, goals, and outcomes matter. In biological agents, that relevance is continually shaped through self-maintenance, embodied action, developmental history, and exposure to the consequences of action. Present language models largely inherit it from humangenerated corpora, training objectives, prompts, evaluation procedures, and deployment institutions. They therefore possess what I call borrowed worldliness: genuine competence acquired from the traces of human engagement with the world, without yet displaying the autonomous normative organization characteristic of ecological agency. Drawing on active inference, ecological psychology, Umwelt theory, and enactivism, the essay develops a substrate-neutral account of this distinction. The argument neither denies the capacities of language models nor rules out artificial agency. It establishes a narrower conclusion: successful inference, even when remarkably general, is not by itself sufficient evidence of an agent for whom anything is at stake.</jats:p>

Mask‐Guided Local Feature Quantization for Small Object Detection
abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quantizing small object detection models is essential for their efficient deployment on edge devices, balancing detection accuracy with inference efficiency. However, existing post‐training quantization methods often damage the fragile high‐frequency features of small objects in low‐bit scenarios. Furthermore, by treating background and target pixels equally, these methods lead to severe performance degradation. To address this issue, we propose a mask‐guided local feature quantization (MLFQ) framework, which reformulates the conventional global‐MSE block reconstruction as a spatially reweighted quantization optimisation. First, we incorporate the adaptive rounding mechanism of AdaRound and the random activation suppression of QDrop to alleviate the local minimum problem in low‐bit quantization. Second, we design a mask‐guided local feature reconstruction loss. This loss utilises a size‐aware spatial weight map, constructed directly from the ground‐truth object scales of the calibration set, decouples quantization error in the spatial dimension, and prioritises the retention of small object features, while introducing no additional inference‐time computation. Experiments against seven representative PTQ baselines on VisDrone‐DET2019 and UAVDT show mixed, marginal differences at W8A8 and W6A6, whereas MLFQ provides its consistent advantage under aggressive W4A4 and W3A3 quantization. We therefore position MLFQ as a low‐bit method and do not claim uniform superiority under every quantization configuration.</jats:p>

Selecting Context for Rule-Grounded Explanation Generation: A Small Language Model Study in Injection Moulding Quality Prediction
abstract: <jats:p>Tree ensembles predict product quality accurately from process-condition data but are opaque, and rule extraction addresses this by compressing an ensemble into a small set of decision rules. A ruleset, however, is a technical representation, and the operators, production managers, and data scientists who act on a quality prediction each require something different from the same ruleset. Small language models deployed on local hardware can express a rule in the terms each audience requires, but they carry little process-specific knowledge and must therefore be grounded in context supplied at inference time. Systems of this kind often supply all available context by default, but the value of this has not been tested. This study presents RuleSLM, which grounds a compact language model in a ruleset extracted from an XGBoost model trained to detect sink mark defects in injection moulding, and decomposes the supplied context into rule evidence, knowledge, and interaction guidance. Crossing the latter two in a factorial design over four small language models and 58 role- and intent-annotated questions shows that interaction guidance increases the evaluator’s role-appropriateness score by 0.323 points on a five-point rubric, that knowledge context changes no dimension measurably, and that the two components interact in opposite directions on different models. Supplying the full context increases the input length by 275% and energy per response by 50% for a benefit confined to one of three quality dimensions. Repeated evaluation further shows that the rubric-based evaluator reproduces fewer than half of the individual scores while producing configuration-by-dimension means that are stable to within 0.12 points. Context for rule-grounded explanation should therefore be selected for the property it serves and validated on the model that will be deployed.</jats:p>

Toward the Dynamics of the Spiral Structure Model: Canonical Quantization, Core Electrodynamics, and the Defect Propagator
abstract: <jats:p>The Spiral Structure Model (SSM) describes the photon as a helical quantum and the electron as a ℤ₂ topological vortex defect of an elastic covariant medium, but its published account is kinematic: the medium’s dynamics was recorded as an open problem. This companion paper reports a concrete candidate dynamics and four derived results. Canonical quantization of the Goldstone (circulation) sector yields an exactly solvable one-quantum problem whose virial theorems return [x, p] = iħ and the SSM momentum width Δp_x = mc/√2. A phase-locking mechanism between the internal circulation and a ξ-scale core texture supplies the two-scale charge structure of the SSM, reduces the self-energy problem by four orders of magnitude, sharpens the core-size bound to ξ ≲ 1.4×10⁻¹⁹ m, and renders the internal excitation band electromagnetically dark (spectral weight ~ 6×10⁻¹²). The gauge sector of the candidate action is QED at one loop, so Schwinger’s a₁ = α/2π is inherited with a definite core-scale deviation; the defect propagator is assembled to the point where its residual failures are quantitative diagnostics rather than open searches; and the elastic vertex follows from the core current with a profile-independent charge radius r_ch = ξ and, for the texture-gradient profile, a diffraction zero at 0.56–4.0 TeV. Finally, the full constraint set on the locked core leaves a global survival window (a factor 65 in the locking stiffness, with walls set by collider and g−2 bounds) and Lorentz covariance of the one-quantum reduction, the one structural gap, is closed: the retarded self-energy kernel supplies (2/3)E₀ of the texture’s inertia where the instantaneous kernel supplies none, the frame-field stress, fixed by the Derrick identity of the soliton sector as the Poincaré-stress analog, supplies the remaining (1/3)E₀, and the von Laue criterion then gives the exact dispersion E(v) = γE₀. The residual open items, the quantum completion of the internal tower and the interaction vertices, are stated with their exact locus of failure.</jats:p>

Asymptotic Equivalence of the Switching Degree with Unknown Boundary — √n-Inference Adaptivity in the Fixed-Breakpoint Model, Finite-Sample Correction Directions, and a Post-Selection Inference Framework
abstract:
<jats:p><p><span>The two-step estimation procedure in structural break detection gives rise to a post-selection inference problem: when the regime boundary is unknown and is first estimated by a test statistic, and the switching degree is then computed on either side of the estimated boundary, the plug-in estimator Ŝ_plug differs from the estimator Ŝ_known obtained with a known boundary. In this paper we prove, in the fixed-breakpoint model (where the switching difference vector Δθ is fixed and nonzero), a core theoretical result: the asymptotic equivalence theorem. Under assumptions A1–A7,</span></p>
<p><span>√n (Ŝ_plug − Ŝ_known) = o_p(1),</span></p>
<p><span>and hence</span></p>
<p><span>√n (Ŝ_plug − S) →_d N(0, V₀),</span></p>
<p><span>exactly as in the known-boundary case. The source of this result is the n-consistency of the boundary estimator in the fixed-breakpoint model: the number of misclassified samples is O_p(1), their effect on the estimated coefficients is O_p(n⁻¹), and this is invisible at the √n scale. Building on this result, we discuss finite-sample correction directions: (i) a first-order heuristic expansion of the conditional bias, indicating that the post-selection bias, although invisible at the √n scale, may be relevant in finite samples; (ii) a fixed-design residual bootstrap scheme, proposed as a working hypothesis, which keeps the design points (Tᵢ, Xᵢ) fixed and resamples only residuals, aiming to mimic the uncertainty of the boundary selection process; (iii) asymmetric bootstrap quantile confidence intervals as a construction proposal. We strictly distinguish proved theorems from unproved working hypotheses. The paper is purely theoretical; numerical validation is an open problem.</span></p>
<p><span>Research Paradigm Statement: The core methodology, research direction, and final decisions were independently directed by the author. DeepSeek assisted with code implementation, data presentation, and text drafting. The author takes full academic responsibility for the final content.</span></p></jats:p>

title: When Does Model Compression Pay Off on a CPU? A Controlled Study of Quantization, Pruning and Distillation for Text Classification
abstract: <jats:p>Compression choices for CPU inference are often made from one benchmark run that reports one accuracy and one latency number per technique. We test how far such numbers can be trusted by compressing a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier on AG News with INT8 dynamic quantization, one-shot magnitude pruning and knowledge distillation, and evaluating every variant on the full 7,600-example test set with bootstrap intervals, paired tests, interleaved repeated timing (batch sizes 1 to 64, one and six threads), a kernel-level analysis, and a distillation grid over student depth, transfer data, loss and random seeds. INT8 quantization shrinks the model by 48% for 0.44 points of accuracy, but its speed benefit depends on the setting: it is 1.9× faster on one thread and slower than FP32 (0.93×) at batch size 1 on six threads, because the INT8 linear kernels barely speed up with more threads at small inputs (1.0 to 1.3× from one to six threads) while FP32 kernels speed up 2.4 to 2.9×. Pruning without retraining is harmless only up to about 19% whole-model sparsity and gives no size or speed benefit in dense tensors. Distillation is what delivers latency: a 2-layer student trained with the teacher's soft labels on 16,000 examples reaches 89.1% accuracy at 3.2 ms against 74.6 ms for the baseline on one thread, and the soft labels are worth 3.6 to 4.8 points over training on labels alone. A first single-run benchmark suggested that a deeper student scores worse; per-seed results show this was an optimization failure, since under fixed hyperparameters five of sixteen 4-layer runs failed (two never started to learn) against none of sixteen 2-layer runs, and with training stabilized the deeper student is still not better. Code and every result file are public.</jats:p>

title: Inference Optimization
Multi-Granularity Reasoning for Natural Language Inference
Integrating Deep Learning and Knowledge Graphs for Natural Language Inference
abstract: <jats:p>Natural Language Inference (NLI) deals with the problem of logical entailment between two sentences. It is evidenced that apart from interpretation of words and syntactic structures, use of external relevant knowledge is also required. This paper investigates whether the integration of external knowledge, represented as triplets and extracted from Knowledge Graphs (KGs), can improve the performance of a pretrained language model on NLI tasks. It also investigates how the source of knowledge affects performance. Six benchmark datasets, namely RTE, QNLI, SICK, SNLI, DNLI, and SciTail, were enriched with knowledge extracted from AristoTuple and WordNet, while ConceptNet was additionally used for the SNLI and SciTail datasets. Enrichment was applied only to the training data through a strict relevance-based selection mechanism using paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and cosine-similarity filtering, and the resulting datasets were used to fine-tune BERT-base-uncased. Evaluation included method-specific configurations selected through validation-based hyperparameter exploration and a controlled multi-seed setting using the vanilla baseline hyperparameters with matched seeds across baseline and enriched datasets. The best observed validation accuracy was 95.24% on SciTail with AristoTuple, while the highest test accuracy, also on SciTail, was 93.70% with ConceptNet. Across both evaluation settings, the effect of knowledge enrichment varied across datasets and knowledge sources, with the multi-seed analysis further assessing the robustness of these effects under controlled training conditions. Overall, the proposed data-level approach achieved competitive performance compared with more complex knowledge-enhanced NLI methods. A taxonomy of existing NLI approaches is also presented.</jats:p>

title: Diagnosing and repairing semantic collapse in small tool-using language-model agents for reliable industrial data analysis
Mapping Linux Auditd Telemetry to MITRE ATT&CK Techniques with a Locally Deployed Small Language Model: A Benchmark on the CAM-LDS Dataset
abstract: <jats:p>Mapping host activity to the MITRE ATT&amp;CK framework usually needs manual work or a cloud-hosted large language model, which raises privacy and cost concerns for small organisations that cannot send their logs off-host. We ask whether a small language model (SLM), running locally and without fine-tuning, can classify Linux auditd records at the technique level of MITRE ATT&amp;CK. We built a deterministic cascade that captures, filters, scores, and aggregates auditd events into session narratives, discarding most records before any model call. Only these narratives reach a quantised SLM (Qwen 2.5 7B, served by Ollama). Candidate techniques are calibrated only on public sources (MITRE ATT&amp;CK, GTFOBins, Sigma), never on the evaluation data. We evaluated the full pipeline on the CAM-LDS dataset, across 29 attack variants, with deterministic and reproducible model outputs under a fixed seed and a temperature of zero. The system reaches a macro-averaged incident-level F1 of 54.2%. Per-variant scores range from 19% to 78%, driven by how much of the attack auditd can observe: scripted attacks leave few visible events, while interactive ones expose far more. An initial pilot with Phi-3 Mini 3.8B produced invalid, hallucinated technique IDs and missed obvious techniques, motivating the switch to Qwen 2.5 7B, which gives the best accuracy–latency trade-off. Our central finding is where the loss happens: the deterministic cascade preserves almost all of the observable on-host activity, so the binding constraints are downstream. The model under-confirms techniques it is given 71% of missed techniques were already available to it and over-broad signatures, not hallucinations, cause most false positives. A local, fine-tuning-free SLM gives a usable technique-level baseline; the ceiling is the model and the catalogue, not the filtering stage.</jats:p>

title: SHAF: Small Language Model Integrated with Motion Modality for Multimodal Interaction
<span>Escaping Rounding Barriers in Large Language Model Quantization via Transverse-Field Ising Optimization</span>
abstract: <jats:p>Weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) pipelines such as AWQ ultimately commit to a deterministic rounding decision for every scalar weight, and recent discrete coordinate-descent quantizers refine those decisions one weight at a time. We show that both are blocked by the same obstacle: correlated activation channels create multi-spin energy barriers in the discrete rounding landscape — configurations in which no single rounding flip helps, yet a small group of coordinated flips strictly reduces the layer reconstruction error. We characterize these barriers exactly under the empirical activation metric and prove that they arise only from frustration between local quantization fields and cross-channel couplings. Building on this analysis we propose Transverse-Field Ising Correction (TFIC), a barrier-aware discrete optimizer that post-processes any AWQ-style pipeline. TFIC casts fixed-grid rounding as a classical Ising ground-state problem, selects the spins near a rounding boundary as a mobile pool, drives that pool to a single-flip local minimum by exact coordinate descent, and then crosses barriers with cluster moves that flip small groups of coupled spins together. Every accepted move is scored against the exact reconstruction energy, and a robust per-layer noise-floor acceptance rule prunes flips whose apparent gain is within calibration-estimation noise; together these guarantee that each layer’s calibration reconstruction error is monotonically non-increasing. TFIC requires no gradients and no architectural changes. On Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B, applying TFIC on top of a 4-bit AWQ baseline consistently reduces WikiText-2 and C4 perplexity, at a per-layer cost of tens of seconds and with no inference-time overhead.</jats:p>
